subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, July 7, consideration of Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, as reported (with amendment) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and Motion No. 13 (Mr. Reynolds).

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Before concluding my speech, I would like to mention by the way, as recorded in Hansard of July 7, 1976, that many government members have been pointing out that we are repeating ourselves. Mr. Speaker, of course we have been repeating ourselves. Why? Merely to make some members understand their irresponsibility in introducing such a measure as Bill C-84 which does away with the security protecting on duty policemen in a country where criminality is constantly increasing. So if we repeat ourselves, as I have just said, it is only to make an individual as irresponsible as the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Allmand) understand that policemen and prison guards can be heard in this Parliament.
It is almost impossible for them to be heard because some members of the opposition and even some government members stubbornly reject clause 4 of the bill before us. I hope that in view of the opposition the government, and the minister in particular, will withdraw clause 4 of the bill. Mr. Speaker, the Solicitor General ought to be sensible enough to realize the uneasiness which exists among police officers and prison guards, since those people must risk their lives every day. This is not a time for philosophy or for hot air, like the Solicitor General seems to think.
Mr. Speaker, one cannot deny that most criminal actions are committed by a small number of individuals whose only purpose it to flout the laws passed by this House. On reading the Journal de Montreal, we see that it is always the same people who commit crimes and who threaten peace and security in Canada.
I quote that paper:
80 per cent of all prisoners are habitual criminals.
On reading things like that, how can we understand that the minister should introduce such a bill? We are told that
about 80 per cent of those who are behind bars in Canada-
10.200	in the provincial institutions of the country and
8.200	in federal penitentiaries-all hardened offenders? Now, to go back to the quotation:
That high percentage is not surprising to anyone who is aware of the traditional weakness of our prisons in the field of rehabilitation, as well as of the obvious hostility of society towards prisoners or former prisoners.
Mr. Speaker, much more could be said about the bill now before the House, and particularly about the amendment moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds). He, at least, understands the opposition of the prison guards and policemen who want to ensure security to the Canadian people in the exercise of their duties.
Mr. Speaker, that is why I shall support this amendment gladly. If the Solicitor General lacks the judgment and common sense to understand the situation, I trust that at least hon. members, even those of the opposition, who are against the amendment, will show enough good will to recognize that prison guards and police agents have good reasons to demand that the death penalty be maintained. Consequently, I intend, on my own behalf and that of my party, for the ridings we represent in Canada, to support this amendment: it is designed to protect the valorous guardians of the peace and public security that police and prison guards are.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to say that there are other representatives from British Columbia here as well. It is a wonderful, large province inhabitated by great people, and it takes a considerable number of members of parliament to represent the people of British Columbia in the way in which they deserve. However, I am honoured to be one of the group from British Columbia.
We are currently discussing amendments to Bill C-84 in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences. The motion proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds), proposes to delete clause 4, and I take the opportunity to indicate my support for the motion. It would retain for policemen and prison guards a measure of safety which presently exists under our ineffective and sloppy administration of justice.
I listened with interest and amazement to the comments made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) yesterday when he stated that while he was in favour of retention of capital punishment, he was going to vote against this motion because it would retain protection for a

July 8, 1976
Criminal Code
certain group of people which was denied to other groups. The hon. member knows very well that this motion is not a discriminatory action on the part of the members who support this motion but is an endeavour to salvage something from the wreckage of a very bad bill proposed by the present government.
It is hardly necessary to remind ourselves of the history of the provision that is being discussed today. It was included in a bill to abolish capital punishment for one reason, that was, I believe, to get the measure through the House of Commons and have it become law. The proposal was that capital punishment be retained for the murder of policemen or prison guards but, as every member of the House is aware this morning, that was just a farce because the government had no such intention at that time, nor has it since that time allowed an execution to be carried out under the provisions of the present legislation. There was a measure of public protest that arose over the inclusion of the exception at that time and many communications came to the desks of all members of parliament, not to object to the protection granted to policemen and prison guards, but to the fact that the same protection was not granted to all the citizens of Canada.
As we look at the facts, we discover that the policemen themselves took exception to the fact that the same protection was not granted to the other citizens of Canada. In a brief, which I am sure every member received, from the Metropolitan Toronto Police Association, we find several brief paragraphs in this connection which I should like to read. On page 15 of the brief we find the following statement:
We must make our position clear with respect to the current law dealing with capital punishment.' It is our contention, clearly and emphatically, that we never proposed, requested nor supported the law as it now stands. In other words, we were not the ones to suggest, request or propose that capital punishment be retained for the killing of police officers, as we are sure neither did the prison officials request capital punishment be retained for the killing of prison officials.
Farther on it says:
We must criticize the current law as being discriminatory in the sense that it places a greater value on the lives of policemen and prison guards than it does on the lives of children, housewives, shopkeepers, businessmen, cab drivers, etc.
Not only do we wish the present law to be retained but we wish it to be expanded to cover the murder of any citizen during the commission of a crime.
I think that is very clear in the presentation of the views of the policemen of this country. So, I wanted to put that on the record to make it clear that this was not a special request made by the policemen or the prison guards of this country. In spite of the fact that protests were raised by citizens, I do not believe that they wanted this clause to be removed. They wanted it to be expanded to include the protection of all Canadians.
Those of us who are speaking on this motion believe that all citizens should be guaranteed the maximum degree of security

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
-that this penalty affords. But if the government is determined to remove this degree of security from society in general and succeeds in doing so, it should be known that we are endeavouring to retain it at

least for those who are charged with the responsibility of ensuring the apprehension and incarceration of criminals in this country.
The policies advocated and put in place by this government have underlined the preoccupation of the government with the so-called rights of the criminal element, to the neglect of the rights of society in general. It seems to me that this motion should carry, so protection could be retained at least for prison guards and policemen. What do we find today? We find that our prison guards are shorn of authority to maintain discipline, and this has been done by government direction. The prison guards have been hassled and insulted by the inmates. They have been deprived of the maximum safety measures. These public servants are working under the severest of handicaps in their efforts to contain the lawbreakers in this nation.
I would like to call attention to a document which has been forwarded to all members of parliament by the Public Service Alliance of Canada. On page 3 there is a reference to a telegram which was forwarded by Mr. J. K. Wylie, executive vice president of the Public Service Alliance of Canada, to Mr. A. Therrien, commissioner of penitentiaries, concerning the measures to protect custodial officers. I would like to quote just one statement made in the reply to that telegram. It was sent by Mr. Therrien, the commissioner. He states, and I quote:
In closing, I wish to assure you most emphatically that the Penitentiary Service considers it of the utmost importance that custodial staff should enjoy secure, peaceful working conditions in which they are able to go about their duties unharrassed and unmolested. The measures I have outlined above are intended to create and maintain a safe environment for personnel, and I am confident that with the co-operation of all concerned, they can be effective in doing so.
I will not take the time to place on the record the statement outlining what has been done, but I do want to point out that I question very much the statements which are made by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), the commissioner of penitentiaries, and others who are trying to insinuate that adequate measures are in place or will be in place to guarantee the safety of the personnel in these institutions. I do not believe that they are sufficient or adequate, and I question very much whether there will be any really effective administration to ensure that the regulations which are now in place will be actually carried out to the fullest extent.
The question then comes to us: what is in store for our penitentiary personnel if and when the legislation is passed and becomes law? Reference has been made to 25 year sentences, but here again there is a catch, and it is quite possible that the exception will become the rule. The clause providing for consideration for parole after 15 years under certain circumstances could become the regular procedure. The precedent that has been set by the government by its actions, including the retention of the death penalty for the murder of certain classes of citizens and then refusing to allow sentences to be carried out, is an indication of what we can expect in the future administration of the law.
I would like to call attention to a portion of the presentation made by the Toronto Policemen's Association in this regard. Page 22 reads, in part:
July 8, 1976

News reports of the new law have left Canadians to believe that if capital punishment is abolished it shall be replaced with a mandatory twenty-five year prison term. Very little, if any, mention is ever drawn to the attention of the public that there is provision for a review of that twenty-five year prison term after fifteen years have been served. Our concern based on past experience is that if capital punishment is abolished in return for longer prison terms, then shortly after the abolishment of capital punishment we will see a lessening of the mandatory jail term and a lessening of the time for a review.
Apparently I am not the only one who questions the credibility of the statements made by the Solicitor General, or even those included in the law, because those who are charged with the responsibility of apprehending criminals-and I believe this feeling is shared by those who are charged with the responsibility of maintaining their incarceration-have very serious questions with regard to the effectiveness of this particular provision.
As I return to the motion which is presently before us to delete from the bill the clause which would remove capital punishment, even as far as the murderers of policemen and prison guards are concerned, I believe this motion warrants the support of the entire House. It certainly should warrant the support of hon. members such as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni because it seems to me that the arguments he used were rather superficial. If he is in favour of the retention of capital punishment for all murderers in the category of first degree murder, or however it may be classified, then he should not withhold that protection from some categories, even if his government insists on removing it for the murder of Canadians in general. So I trust that when this motion is brought before the House for a final decision, it will receive the unanimous support of all hon. members of this House and that capital punishment, at least for the murderers of prison guards and policemen, will be retained in our legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to make a few remarks on that extremely important clause of the bill, because if there is a subject which should spur the conscience of all hon. members of the House, it is indeed this bill, and particularly clause 4.
Mr. Speaker, when we think about the role policemen have to play in Canada, we realize the full significance of the legislation before us. We know to what extent our municipal officials and our Canadian police associations at various levels rightly insist on the dedication, the competence and the respectability of our policemen. We even require a very high level of education for an applicant to be accepted in any police force. Courses are given every year in all provinces to our different police forces to ensure public protection, because the policeman, for any normal Canadian, should ensure public protection. That is why he is highly paid. This is why we now see policemen earning $15,000, $18,000 and even $20,000 a year. We are spending staggering amounts for our police salaries so that people may receive the best possible protection.
But while we are asking the police to ensure public safety we, in return, do not want to ensure police safety. We want our policemen to protect us but Parliament does not want to protect them. I cannot imagine more stupid, more inane legislation than the one which is before us. We are paying security forces to protect us, our children, our society, the taxpayers and their properties. We are asking
Criminal Code
the police to fulfill its role, namely to ensure the security of society; that is what we are paying for. On the other hand, the House of Commons refuses to grant those policemen the very protection they are expected to give the public. It is outrageous that this government has reached such a stage. In the final analysis, it means the present government is trying to bring this country to the brink or anarchy. From the moment we do not want to give any protection to the individuals who receive large amounts of money to protect us, this means, Mr. Speaker, that we are ready to live in anarchy in Canada as of tomorrow morning.
Mr. Speaker, we also expect policemen to be well educated and to drive good cars, we ask them to have good systems to fight fire, we also require our prison guards to be well equipped; nevertheless, the first facility we must give policemen is the opportunity to protect themselves, to protect their own lives. We must put ourselves today in the situation of the policemen who have to respond to a telephone call saying that a hold-up is in progress in a bank on the corner of a given street and that someone has already been shot by the bandits who broke into the bank. In the city of Acton Vale, we saw a notorious bandit, who had been swearing for years he would get rid of the police chief, take advantage of a fight in a hotel one evening to shoot this police chief in front of witnesses standing by, something like 200 people. The police chief of Acton Vale was the father of nine children.
How do policemen feel while they are waiting in the police station for distress calls from the public? How do they feel when they must take over after their chief has been shot by a bandit, when they are asked to protect them while they themselves are not even armed and protected, in the sense that it will not matter if the same bandit, who just shot the chief, guns down his assistant or other policemen because there is no punishment, because he is on the same social footing and enjoys the same credibility as the chief of police who had to submit references and a clean record. The bandit who just shot the chief of police, and who already committed many murders is put before society on the same footing as this policeman.
Mr. Speaker, I am shocked to hear such an argument from a member who asks for the protection of policemen, and who refuses today to give them such protection. I have here the summary of the brief submitted by the national police committee. We must consider it because those concerned today are the policemen. We should have consideration for those who are bound to fight criminals rather than take the advice of political scientists, sociologists or demagogues who hide behind the Solicitor General, who have probably never seen a gangster in their life but who are good at counselling or advising the minister. The minister should choose policemen and nobody else as advisers because they are the ones who are concerned with clause 4. But as long as the government is going to sit and listen to public servants who have no responsibility in running the country, we are likely to be faced once again with bills as stupid and childish as the one before us today.
Mr. Speaker, I understand the position of our policemen. Why are they so disgusted today to see that parliamentarians refuse them the same protection they have always

granted us? I know dozens of police forces in Canada and more particularly those in my riding. They have a conscientious approach to their work in providing public protection. They protect our children, our students and our properties which they defend with eagerness in spite of the risks. We call them to lend assistance to threatened people and to some organizations. They are called in case of fire, for instance, the same way the fire fighters are called, but they are policemen whose services are used to help the people when fire breaks out.
And today we have before us a bill which tends to deprive policemen of protection. I find that disgusting and I find that those who are going to remove the protection for policemen are without conscience. They want to deprive policemen of protection and at the same time they demand police protection. I can only feel revolted by this legislation which should never have been put before the House. And here is what policemen say about the Solicitor General:
We disagree with the minister when he says that it is up to retention-ists to show why the legislation should not be changed. According to us . . .
They are policemen, they are not all fools, not all civil servants sitting in an office who never had to face criminality ...
the minister is the one who should prove .. .
They are not listened to, the representations made in Canada by police forces are not taken into account, some of us would rather listen to representations made by criminals and those who have to do with crime.
According to us, the minister is the one who should prove that the legislation must be changed . ..
That is good logic. The minister is the one who should prove that the legislation must be changed, that is what policemen say.

We object to the public statement by the highest judiciary authority in Canada that he would resign if capital punishment were to be carried out.
Mr. Speaker, how can someone make such a childish public statement? A real child! If he does not get a toy, if he does not get a candy, he is going to go into tantrum. The minister has said that he would resign if anyone should hang. And this statement emanates from the highest judiciary authority in the country! He is the one responsible for the implementation of the law. And he would resign if his bill were not accepted. The brief goes on:
What if all law officers in Canada had this attitude regarding the laws they do not like to enforce?
If law officers were to have this attitude, Mr. Speaker, there would be a general strike overnight by all police forces in Canada because police officers now have to enforce laws they do not like, and yet they do not voice such irresponsible and stupid remarks as those expressed by the minister who said recently that he will resign if his bill is defeated.
We are worried by the public statements of the Solicitor General reflecting his intention to propose a reduced term after which murderers would be eligible for parole following the abolition of capital punishment.

If the Solicitor General really believes that neither the state nor any individual or institution has the right to take a life, we can then expect that he will soon propose that Canadian policemen be unarmed lest they might kill someone in the course of their duties.
What action did the minister take to accommodate the large number of murderers . ..
It sounds good to say that those people will be sent to jail, but our current pentitentiary system in Canada prevents us from putting those people behind bars because we do not have enough jails, enough facilities and the minister knows it. No plans have been made yet to implement what is suggested in this bill: send murderers to jail for 25 years. Jails are already filled to capacity.
What plans did the minister make to accommodate the large number of murderers who will be sentenced to 25 years if the bill is passed in its present form? We are told that jails are already overcrowded, obsolete and are nothing but rest homes. How will these institutions and their authorities be able to face the flow of convicts sentenced to long terms?
Mr. Speaker, what do the policemen think of the deterrent effect?
The executed murderer cannot commit a second crime.
The fact that violent riots in prisons have caused the death of inmates and injuries to guards shows positively the deterrent effect of the capital punishment threat.
Mr. Speaker, about 500 feet from my home, two prison guards have witnessed last year the murder of their colleagues in the Cowansville jail. Presently, those people are on leave without pay because they suffer from a nervous breakdown after they realized what happens inside jails because of the lack of protection given to prison guards. Those people are still on welfare. They received a salary for some time and, today, their doctor gave them a medical certificate: nervous breakdown. It is not the minister, the Solicitor General who risks his life in prisons, without any tools, without any means of protection.
We recommend to the members of the justice committee to consider the findings of a study conducted by Ehrlich and Yunker of the United States, as well as the verbatim report that the American Attorney General filed with the Supreme Court of that country dealing with capital punishment and the constitution of the USA. It is interesting to note that out of the 50 states, 37 have now passed legislation on capital punishment. We are convinced that if we want to compare our jurisdiction with others, it would be more helpful to compare it with that of the USA, because it is more relevant to Canadian jurisdiction than any other in this world.
We take pleasure in this House in wanting to copy the legislation of countries that live under socialist governments, but we should be more inclined to imitate our next door neighbour whose methods we copy every day in the field of trade and in every other activity, except that of justice.
We think that the punishment should be proportional to the crime committed. To us that is justice, not revenge, nor retribution-justice.
Justice is not set by administrators, policemen or legislators. Justice is set by the acceptance by Canadians of the degrees of punishment and their relation to the seriousness of the crime committed.
The results of countless surveys indicate that the majority of Canadians demand justice for murder. The justice they demand is that capital punishment be maintained and that it be applied to premeditated murders, or murders committed during the perpetration of a crime.
That is signed by the Canadian Police Association, by the president, the vice-president and the past president.
I could also read what was done in England:
Return to hanging for murder or genuine life imprisonment.
July 8, 1976

While all Great Britain police departments are going through the country with a fine toothcomb looking for dangerous murderers, the widow of a recently slain chief of police launched a massive campaign in favour of the reinstatement of hanging in England.
"If the country were at war nobody would be offended that death would be the fate of the enemy and I think we are at war with criminals," said pretty Maureen Richardson, a 35 year old brunette.
Her husband, Superintendent Gerald Richardson was gunned down with several shots as he was attempting to arrest two bandits who were trying to flee after stealing jewelry estimated at over $120,000 in Blackpool.
The police identified Richardson's assassin as being Frederick Joseph Sewell, age 34 or 36; this would be his second murder.
Forbes had escaped last Monday from the Peterhead prison in Scotland. He would be the first individual in the judicial annals of Scotland to be guilty of a second murder after being paroled on a sentence of life imprisonment.
That is what the Solicitor General's policy will lead us to with paroles and 25-year terms. Because after a few months, we have seen that individuals commit one, two, three or four murders.
It goes on to state:
Commenting on her campaign, Mrs. Richardson indicated: "I urge reinstatement of hanging for premeditated murders, and I stress that anybody who puts a loaded revolver in his pocket is premeditating something".
Also, as my hon. colleague from Moncton (Mr. Jones) suggested, and I quote:
The Maritimes police officers urge for a return to capital punishment.
This is what Senator Robichaud indicated, and things become serious when a senator suggests he is going to make his own justice.
Senator Louis Robichaud, former premier of New Brunswick, suggested he was opposed to violence under any form but could not accept the way the parole boards and the judicial system let murderers go unpunished in a number of instances. "If someone rapes and kills my daughter, and if adequate punishment is not inflicted by the judiciary, I will personally make it my duty to apply punishment". Such were his words.
Mr. Speaker, when we hear a senator going on record to say he will protect himself, what can we expect from police forces in Canada when they find they have no protection anymore? They will be considered just as criminals are. They will be afforded the same kind of respect given gangsters who perpetrated three, four or even five murders. We will see criminals put on the same social footing as a chief of police with credibility and an impeccable record. Police chiefs are men of talent and character, they often have very important responsibilities outside their official function, as some I have known in my own constituency. At this point in his conscience, the Solicitor General is placing the gangster and the chief of police on an equal footing before the law.
The Quebec Association of Police Directors is fed up with the way the parole board behaves; they blame it for being too generous toward recidivists.
Recidivists are awarded medals! I wonder why, in his bill, the minister did not ask that bandits and criminals be given credit cards and Cadillac cars to better rehabilitate those poor souls into our society.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on motion No. 13 brought forward by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds). The amendment calls for the deletion of clause 4 of Bill C-84, the clause which would repeal the present provisions of section 214 of the Criminal Code and substitute the penalty of life imprisonment for first degree murder. In effect this would mean a penalty of 25 years in the case of a first conviction for the murder of a police officer, prison guard or correctional officer. I support the amendment because if this clause were deleted we would go back to the law as it was.
I wish to refer to an excellent article by Michael Marley in today's Montreal Gazette in which he comments on the convoluted thinking of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on the death penalty. I quote:
It is because I have an enduring confidence in mankind (the law-abiding sort) and confidence in society's ability to protect itself (if it is given the chance) that I favor retention of capital punishment.
This is certainly a volatile enough issue for a general referendum. The government should either give us one or resign and allow us to choose leaders who will be less autocratic and more responsive to the desires of the population.
I agree with Mr. Marley that the government should resign. However, I do not think there is any need for a referendum. There have been many polls taken in Canada as well as questionnaires and letters to members of parliament. We already know the views of the Canadian people.
On April 30, 1975, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) presented a petition. At that time he said, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition on capital punishment on behalf of over 200,000 concerned people across Canada- a very small percentage of the overall majority who are in favour of capital punishment. May I say the petitions forms were made available in both official languages across Canada.
I understand the end result was that this petition finally had about one million signatures. That in itself should give this government something to think about. It is another reason for them to consider supporting motion No. 3.
There was another article which appeared earlier this year headed "Gospel church poll is 90 per cent in favour of death penalty". I quote:
A Hamilton minister wrote to Canada's Solicitor-General yesterday calling for the retention of the death penalty, based on a survey of the membership of the Associated Gospel Churches of Canada.
It will be found that many opinion polls reached 90 per cent in favour of the death penalty although the overall average for Canada is 75 per cent.
95570-58V2

July 8, 1976
Criminal Code
On February 2, 1976, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) issued a news release containing the results of a questionnaire sent to his constituents. It stated that no fewer than 73 per cent of the citizens of Ottawa West favoured retention of capital punishment. Because of his actions there, in all probably the hon. member for Ottawa West will return to this House after the next election.
We cannot ignore the presentations we received from police associations and prison guards. I wish to read into the record a letter that was sent to the Prime Minister, copies of which were sent to all members of parliament. I quote:
The Canadian Police Association, which represents 40,000 municipal and provincial police officers in Canada, met in Toronto in February 1975 to discuss the issue of capital punishment. The Association is deeply concerned over the fact that there is now no penalty of consequence imposed on persons who commit murder in our country. Persons convicted of murder who are given a "life" sentence can be eligible for parole in seven to ten years after conviction. It is the view of the policemen of this country, as represented by the association, that this is not a suitable penalty and does not serve to protect society.
There have been some changes with regard to the length of sentence, but that is not what the Canadian people want.
In July 1972 the Association informed the Honourable John Turner, then Minister of Justice, of our position with respect to capital punishment; a copy of the submission setting out our position was forwarded to you as well. Our recommendations were ignored by your government.
The government is not only ignoring the police association and the guard's association, but between 80 and 90 per cent of the Canadian people.
In July 1973 the association wrote to the Honourable James Jerome, Chairman of the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee of the House of Commons, advising him and his committee of our views on the issue of capital punishment. Once again our recommendations were ignored.
It is our belief that our position, as outlined to the government in 1972 and reiterated in 1973, is even more applicable in 1975 since crimes of violence continue to plague this country at an alarming rate and since the penalties imposed by present legislation are no deterrent.
We recognize that it is the responsibility of police officers to enforce the law and that it is the responsibility of government and parliament to make the laws which police officers must enforce. However, the law must serve to protect the citizen and it is the view of the Canadian Police Association that the present laws with respect to punishment for murder are inadequate and fail to provide for the proper protection of Canadian citizens.
It is our belief that unless substantial steps are taken to provide meaningful penalties for the murder of our citizens the rate of these violent crimes will continue to escalate.
The Canadian Police Association is again advancing to members of parliament the position they take with respect to capital punishment and are advising the Canadian people of this position so that citizens can be aware of the concern felt by their police officers in every province in Canada.
The Canadian Police Association strongly recommends that the government of Canada immediately review the present laws pertaining to punishment for murder, in line with the following resolution:
"Capital punishment must be extended beyond the present limitations so as to include all crimes in which acts of violence result in the death of any person.
Persons who take the life of another while committing such crimes as child molestation, rape, air piracy, political assassination, treason, and robbery must be charged with capital murder and, if convicted, should face the death penalty.
In cases where persons are found guilty of capital murder, after all levels of judicial appeal have been exhausted, and no recommendation for mercy is forthcoming from the judicial process, the federal 
cabinet shall be prohibited from interfering with that sentence and subsequent punishment.
In cases where a recommendation for mercy is forthcoming from the judicial process the federal cabinet should be permitted to commute the death sentence. However the alternative to the death sentence should be limited to natural or true life imprisonment."
We, the police officers who have sworn to serve and protect the citizens of Canada, firmly believe that all law abiding citizens have a right to expect, and indeed to demand, to be able to live in peace and safety, free from fear of criminal acts being perpetrated against them or against member of their families. The continued eroding of this feeling of security by elected representatives, through their failure adequately to maintain legislation guaranteeing every reasonable protection to all law abiding citizens, is of the greatest danger to our free society; if allowed to continue, this erosion will ultimately destroy our accepted way of life.
The letter is signed by S. R. Scarr, the president of the association. I might point out that the police association has the support of the majority of Canadians. I find it strange that this government continually ignores these types of requests, as well as representations received from constituents across Canada.
Members of parliament received a letter from the Public Service Alliance of Canada dated June 24, 1976, which reads as follows:
Before you cast your final ballot on Bill C-84, we would like to bring to your attention the following facts so that in conscience, as you were reminded by the Prime Minister of Canada in his address to the House on June 15, 1976, appearing in the Commons Debates, page 14499, and I quote "I want to make it very clear that, if a majority of honourable members vote against abolition, some people are going to be hanged. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a further opportunity to speak on this important subject because I believe we are dealing with a critical aspect of our whole system of law and order when we address ourselves to this motion. We have an opportunity before us now to uphold that system at least to a degree by affording to police and prison officers the protection which many Canadians are demanding.
Prison guards and policemen are, by the very nature of their work, in contact most of the time with lawbreakers and the criminal element of our society. In other words, their chances of being attacked or murdered are very much greater than those of the average citizen. This being the case, they deserve special protection. We owe it to policemen and prison guards to provide them with every reasonable protection we can offer. In recent times we have seen an alarming increase in the taking of hostages both inside and outside prisons, an exercise often designed to make possible the escape or release of inmates held in prison. Such incidents will probably have serious consequences for us in the future and will, undoubtedly, result in the murder of prison guards.
Those who take on jobs as police officers and prison guards are fathers and husbands just like anyone else. When they undertake to make a career as policemen or in prison work they recognize there are certain risks attached to their decision. The question here is how high this risk ought to be. Surely, men and women who embark on a career in this type of work should be able to enjoy a normal life expectancy. We are increasing substantially the risks run by these public servants if we fail to pass the amendment before us.
One of the immediate concerns affecting police forces across the country is whether they will be able in future to recruit sufficient men of high calibre, such as we are privileged to have in our police forces at the present time, to meet the needs of our law enforcement requirements. At the present time, for example, I am advised that the Calgary police force is experiencing great difficulty in meeting its recruitment needs in spite of the fact that pay for policemen in Calgary is No. 4 in Canada and that fringe benefits are equal to the best. The pressure is already beginning to be felt. The removal of capital punishment to
Criminal Code
the extent indicated in this motion is likely to have serious effects in terms of police reaction and morale.
I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that last winter, following the killing of policemen in the province of Quebec, there was a strong likelihood of the entire Quebec provincial police force going out on strike in protest. A few years ago, in Montreal, when the police decided to walk out the result was chaos. If we remove this important protection from the law we are inviting a reaction from our police forces every time there is a brutal slaying of a policeman in this country. We have all witnessed the paralysing effect of a walk-out by airline pilots. I ask hon. members to consider the effect of a police walk-out, whether in a city or in a province, or of a walk-out by prison guards.
The government, either on purpose or by bad management, seems to have pitted almost every conceivable group in our society against another ever since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to power. They have set labour against business, rich against poor, French against English, and in this case law-abiding citizens against the government. If there were to be a widespread walk-out by police or prison guards, or a tide of resignations, the result could be the imposition of martial law in this country.
Why is the removal of the death penalty for any and every possible offence necessary or desirable? The government across the way is directly responsible for the deterioration of law and order in Canada. Its permissive actions and the changes it has made in the law have brought about a much worse society than we had hoped for or deserved. Under this administration, the man who obeys the law, the man who works for his living, is taking a back seat to the law breaker, to those who will not work and to those who are encouraged to live off the system. The removal of protection for our police forces as prescribed in the bill before us is another step backward, a step toward anarchy.
I wish the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) would tell us more about the trial period in connection with abolition which began in 1967 and which was extended in 1973. What trial was conducted? What scientific evidence was gathered? Why did the minister ask the House to extend the trial period a short 32 months ago? What further evidence does the government require? What further evidence did they get? Mr. Speaker, the so-called trial period was not a trial period at all. The whole exercise was a farce. Since the law of Canada was never carried out, no one was ever hanged for the killing of a policeman or a prison guard. There was no deterrent, no experiment. We have, in effect, been living with the complete abolition of capital punishment since the Prime Minister took office.
This example of lawbreaking and disregard for the wishes and feelings of the people is a matter of national concern. The government seems to believe that laws are to be passed with no regard whatsoever for the wishes of the people. It will learn that as a result of this arrogance and disregard it will be thrown out of office. Governments and members of this House, no matter what anyone says, are here to speak for their constituents, and when they do not the voters find representatives who will speak for them. I know that members opposite are under tremendous pressure from their constituents. I understand this is particularly the case with members from the province of Quebec. It is interesting that their leader has so much influence on

July 8, 1976
Criminal Code
those opposite that they listen to him and not to their constituents.
Capital punishment in the United States is an example which cannot be overlooked. The Supreme Court ruled very recently that the death penalty is not a cruel or unusual punishment. Thus, the death penalty can and will be imposed by many more states. Some 37 states have returned to the death penalty and it is expected now that many more, in fact most states in the United States will.
If we do not uphold capital punishment in respect of the killing of prison guards and policemen, I would ask you to consider what are the consequences for our Canadian police forces which are considered to be basically conservative groups of men. If we remove this important protection from the law in respect of our police officers, and they are faced every day and night with investigations, checking out people in automobiles and strange, dark places, they are going to step out with their guns drawn. I can assure you that they are going to shoot first and shoot to kill if there is any question about their own security or their own lives. There will be no trial and no jury. The action will be all over. In addition to that, it is clear today, although it may not have been a few years ago, that in such instances these police officers who kill in the carrying out of their duty will have the full support of the Canadian people.
I think it is important to put on record the fact that since this experiment of partial abolition, which truly has been complete abolition, there have been 37 policemen and three prison guards killed in our country. If we consider the statements made by the Solicitor General even in the last few weeks, we see that he has made it very clear in his speeches around the country that he intends to alter the commitment he is apparently making that the 25-year imprisonment provision will be enforced in respect of those convicted for first-degree murder. It is very clear from the history of this government and the statements of the minister that they will very soon start to whittle and chip away at this proposed punishment so that it will be just a matter of time until it is reduced to 20 years, 15 years or perhaps even 10 years.
The Solicitor General has a very important place in this whole matter of law enforcement in our country. He answers to parliament for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, for the prisons and penitentiaries of our country. When it is clear that the prison personnel and, certainly privately, members of the RCMP do not agree and take a very strong reaction against the bill, specifically the removal of this clause to protect prison guards and policemen as referred to in the amendment we are now discussing, then it becomes clear he has lost the confidence of those to whom he is supposed to show leadership. If this clause of the bill is defeated, then I think the Solicitor General has no alternative but to resign his position as Solicitor General.
In closing, I wish once more to refer to this question of capital punishment and whether it is a deterrent. This has constantly been the question raised by hon. members opposite and by the Prime Minister. A constituent of mine, Mr. R. G. Campbell, has stated, as have so many, that the

question of capital punishment is one in respect of which each person's opinion is just as valid as the next. The claim of some privileged, or some special knowledge or understanding which is made by hon. members opposite that apparently is not available to Canadians at large is the basis of an absolutely foolish and ridiculous argument.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak in support of the amendment to Bill C-84 in relation to capital punishment for the murderers of policemen and prison guards, presented by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds). I was not going to enter this debate until I heard the speech of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson). He claims to be a retentionist, but during his speech he said he would not support this amendment because it would make second-class citizens of many Canadians. I really do not understand the logic or the rationalization of that hon. member, if in fact he is a retentionist.
I heard this argument used during the last debate we had in respect of a further five-year experiment to abolish capital punishment with the exception of cases involving
July 8, 1976

the murder of policemen and prison guards. The people who put this argument forward were, of course, in favour of the retention of capital punishment for everyone, but they certainly agreed most emphatically that there should be capital punishment for anyone who murders a policeman or prison guard.
Now we are speaking about the total abolition of capital punishment and we have already had one vote in which those people who are in favour of abolition won by a very slim margin. A retentionist argues now that he will not support this motion, which is the very motion we should favour, that there be capital punishment for the murderers of policemen and prison guards. How can anyone rational-' ize his position and say he will not support the motion because it will make second-class citizens of people who are not policemen or prison guards? How can this position be rationalized thus?
The motion put forward by the hon. member for Burna-by-Richmond-Delta is essential for the maintenance of law and order in Canada. The government came forth with what they call a peace and security package in Bill C-83 and Bill C-84 which they said would bring better law and order to this country. When we were able to analyze these two pieces of legislation, together with the people of Canada, we found we could not buy this package which, as the government said, would bring better law and order. Bill C-83 deals mostly with gun control. It will not do much to control guns in the hands of criminals; it could even make criminals out of people who have guns. The people of Canada quickly saw through this and the majority of them continue to favour retention of capital punishment. In my view, there are more people in favour of capital punishment since this package was presented than there were before. Before these two bills were put forward, well over 50 per cent were in favour of capital punishment, whereas now nearly 80 per cent favour it.
There was a five-year experiment in retaining capital punishment for the murder of policemen and prison guards only. A bill was presented a second time, which received less acceptance in the House, extending the experiment for a further two years. We know that during that time 37 policemen were murdered in Canada and three prison guards. These are the kinds of results that the people of Canada are looking at. Canadians want law and order in Canada, which they do not have under the present government.
The work of our policemen and prison guards should be made easier, and this is what the amendment before us attempts to achieve. Those of us who are retentionists, as well as those who are abolitionists, should look closely at this amendment and be ready to vote in favour of it. By taking away the last line of protection that policemen and prison guards have, we are making their jobs that much harder. People who are looking for jobs in Canada, the very people whom the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) wants to put to work, will not be interested in obtaining that kind of employment which affords them no protection, where they have to put their lives on the line at all times. The government will have a hard time recruiting people for these jobs.
Criminal Code
We know that many prison guards who have been working at their jobs for a long time and who know much more about that work than we as parliamentarians do, are saying they will not be happy in their jobs if this bill passes unamended, and in fact they will be ready to retire early or find some other work. To replace them we will have to find another group of people; but they, also, will find these jobs hazardous, especially when they hear people who do not respect law and order saying, "Let's go out and get a policeman tonight". Policemen are very aware of this situation and aware of the hazards of their jobs.
I say we should make our policemen and prison guards proud of their profession and proud of the opportunity to carry out law and order. We should provide protection for them so that they do not have to be worried about their lives. I say to every member of the House-and especially to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni-that they should look at this amendment which would provide better protection for policemen and prison guards. It is a good amendment to Bill C-84. I am certainly in support of it and I hope the amendment will be accepted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate in support of the motion which is before us and which proposes that clause 4 of Bill C-84 be deleted. If I may, first of all I would like to outline why I am most anxious that hon. members consider allowing the death penalty to remain with respect to the killing of jail guards and policemen. If we read Bill C-84, it is very disturbing to find that the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand) proposes that a man may be convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment and can literally be out on the streets-granted, with an escort-within a day for various lengths of time. I draw the attention of hon. members to clause 21 of the bill, which appears at page 12. It proposes an amendment to section 674 of the Criminal Code, and I refer specifically to section 674(2) which provides:
Notwithstanding the Penitentiary Act and the Parole Act, in the case of any person sentenced to imprisonment for life without eligibility for parole for a specified number of years pursuant to this act. no absence without escort may be authorized under the Penitentiary Act-
, It specifies that this will be the case until there are only three years to run of the full sentence. In short, what the Solicitor General is suggesting is that even where a person is convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment, under certain circumstances he may be permitted to leave jail provided he has an escort.
Let us consider those circumstances, because this is what I find most disturbing. We find that absence with an escort is dealt with in another bill which is before is, Bill C-83. In that bill it is clearly set out that if someone is incarcerated, he may be temporarily absent with an escort under two different circumstances. The first is that the Commissioner of Penitentiaries, for an unlimited period of time for medical reasons and for a period not exceeding 15 days for humanitarian reasons or to assist in the rehabilitation of the inmate, may grant leave with an escort to anyone in jail. Second, and this is what I find most disturbing, any officer in charge of a jail, for a period not exceeding 15 days for medical reasons and for a period not exceeding

July 8, 1976
Criminal Code
five days for humanitarian reasons, or to assist in the rehabilitation of the inmate, may allow an inmate to be absent from jail provided he has an escort.
I have mentioned that the person in charge of a jail may permit an inmate to leave for five days. I point out that under the existing act it is only three days. However, the Solicitor General is proposing in Bill C-83, that such a person be given two extra days leave or the right to be absent, provided he has an escort.
I think the misrepresentation which has taken place with respect to the so-called life sentence which the government is proposing is most unfair to the Canadian public. The Solicitor General should have made it abundantly clear that there is no life sentence in the context in which that term is usually used. Abolitionists have said to me, in referring to life sentences, that they generally think of a Devil's Island type of situation where a man is convicted and for 25 years, come what may, he stays shut off from society and there is no way he can get back into society. In effect, the key is thrown away.
Let us be clear; that is not what the government is proposing in the bill before us. It is suggesting that even where a person is convicted of murder he will be sentenced to a term of life, or 25 years, which is open to review in 15 years, but let us bear in mind that during that period even for the first 12 years he can be absent from prison as long as he has an escort. Who is the escort to be? The escort is to be a policeman or some other peace officer as defined in the act. I think that is an extremely dangerous provision.
As hon. members know, I am proposing that the Solicitor General's amendment to the Criminal Code contained in Bill C-84 be amended, because I believe that under no circumstances should a person be permitted to leave jail, even with an escort, without further review or confirmation that there is a minimum of danger. My amendment suggests that absence with an escort should not be granted unless there is a judge's order. I have discussed this with the minister. He points out that the wording may be ambiguous. With that I agree, and subsequently a colleague of mine will be moving a further amendment to my amendment to make clear exactly what we are trying to achieve. We are saying that there should be no absence without an escort, under any circumstances, but that absence with an escort must only be with the approval of a judge or, as has been suggested, perhaps with the approval of the National Parole Board. That will be the tenor of our amendment to be introduced subsequently.
I was a little startled when the hon. member who spoke before me referred to the remarks which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) made yesterday. Speaking on the amendment which is before us, namely, the retention of the death penalty for murderers of prison guards and policemen, the hon. member stated that, while he is a retentionist, he felt it unfair to have the death penalty for what he though was a select group of society. He wonders why policemen are different from others. He stated, as reported at page 15133 of Hansard;
I believe that the murder of a policeman or a prison guard is no more, or no less, important than the killing of a child, a fisherman or any other member of our society ... I still feel that this is a discriminatory provision, and the sooner we get rid of the idea that some groups in society are more important than others, the better off we will be.
[Mr. Stevens.)
I am not saying that the death penalty should not be extended to many more classes of murder than simply the killing of a jail guard or a policeman, but I do say that the hon. member is quite wrong in saying that policemen should not have the added protection which the death penalty provides. I say that because we must accept that policemen, contrary to what the hon. member says, unlike firemen and unlike most people in society, are charged with the preservation of our whole system of law and order. They are the front-line troops, so to speak, and I think this parliament must do everything in its power to ensure that they are respected when they are on duty.
Perhaps one of the main reasons I feel so strongly about the retention of the death penalty is that when I was a reporter for the Toronto Daily Star, many times I had the opportunity to be with the police when they brought in people who were involved in crime. I remember very vividly that day in March, 1952, when two detectives were shot down in the city of Toronto by Steven Suchan and Leonard Jackson. I think if any member of the House had witnessed what transpired before that shooting, what transpired after the shooting and what happened afterwards as far as the police were concerned in rounding up the two convicts, they would be a lot less sure that they should vote for abolition.
Perhaps many hon. members do recall that shooting. Sergeant detective Edmund Ton died 17 days later, and his assistant detective sergeant Roy Perry was wounded and recovered but could take no part in active police work and occupied a desk job for the rest of his days on the force. He is now dead. I mention this because I remember the night they finally cornered Leonard Jackson in Toronto. I remember the apprehension of the police as they left police headquarters to try to arrest Leonard Jackson. I remember Jackson's statement, hollered from the house he was in, that the police would have to come and get him. They did, Mr. Speaker. I remember the account of what happened in Montreal when Steven Suchan was cornered in his apartment. The police had to go in with guns drawn. He was shot as he tried to shoot the police who went into the apartment.
I believe for members of the House to suggest that policeman should not be given the added protection of making it clear to a criminal that if he dare shoot a policeman or a prison guard he, in turn, will lose his life is to let down our police force and prison guards. In fact, I think the government must carry a heavy weight through insisting that this legislation be passed.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), perhaps feeling that there was not sufficient support for this bill, stated in this House that members should keep in mind that if they voted against this bill and it did not pass, some people in this country would hang. I say, let the Prime Minister remember that to the degree he insist and his cabinet colleagues insist that this bill be passed, every future murder in this country is on their hands to the degree that it could have been deterred. While the government weighs the fate of the 11 people who are now sentenced to die, while they hesitate to commute, hoping that this legislation will be passed and then they will not have to take that position, I say to hon. members that since the death penal-
July 8, 1976

ty was abolished, to all intents and purposes, 65 people in this country have been sentenced to die. Of that number, 54 death sentences have been commuted and 11 are awaiting the decision of the government and the passage of this bill.
As we weigh the possibility of whether these people should be legally executed or not, let us not forget that in the same period over 4,000 Canadians were illegally executed. They were the victims of this type of crime. I think it would have served the Prime Minister better to have pointed out that retention of the death penalty, at least in a limited sense and certainly for prison guards and policemen, may help to deter future murderers, and if in any way we can lower the death rate from murder in this country, we should. I think the government is not acting responsibly and I call upon hon. members to support this amendment on that point alone.
The government likes to raise the question of how some of our members have voted. Have hon. members on the government side noticed that in the second reading vote on this matter, 80 per cent of the Conservative caucus voted for retention?

The other point I would make-and obviously government members are confused about it-is that this is represented by the government as a free vote. The free vote is on this side of the House and we, to the extent of 80 per cent, voted for retention. I think it is a credit to our caucus that we were allowed that freedom of vote.
I have touched briefly on why I believe this amendment should be supported and why we should allow the death penalty to continue with regard to the killing of prison guards and policemen. I should like to back this up with some statistics. It is often stated-I notice the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) said that somehow what I was saying was totally different from what the Prime Minister was saying-that it is a deterrent to have the death penalty.
On January 26, 1973, at page 688 of Hansard, speaking on Bill C-2-which was the old version of Bill C-84-the Solicitor General stated that he would like to have three six-year periods to compare with respect to three ap-
Criminal Code
proaches to capital punishment, and at the end of that time he could decide whether the death penalty should be eliminated permanently. The minister said, in 1973:
We are just receiving the statistics for 1971. It seems to me that we must see the process, commenced in 1967, through to its logical conclusion. That further necessitates making no substantial change in the law until such time as we are in a position to fully understand the impact of the partial abolition. Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members. The first period was between 1956 and 1962. I am referring to Statistics Canada figures regarding murders. The average number of murders per 100,000 of population during the first six-year period, when the death penalty not only was on the statute books but criminals were executed was 1.1 in Canada. I have referred to Jackson and Suchan in Toronto who were executed in December of the year they committed the crime. In the next six years, while in theory the death penalty was still in force in this country, in practice every sentence was commuted and there was no death penalty. In that period the murder rate rose to 1.5 per
100,000	population. Now let us look at the last six years. As the minister said when speaking on second reading, last year the murder rate in Canada had risen to 2.4 per 100,000 population, a rate more than double that applying to the 1956 to 1962 period.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE

speechtext: And what about other serious crimes?

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: The hon. member asks, what about other serious crimes? That is a strange twist. The hon. member should realize that our crime rate is rising because the government is taking a more lenient attitude to those who commit crime.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext: It is too permissive.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Those guilty of the most serious of all crimes, murder, should be punished with death; only then will people realize that this government means business. I emphasize that I am not making an emotional argument. Statistics show clearly the rising murder rate in this country and elsewhere. Faced with such a rise in the murder

July 8, 1976
Criminal Code
rate, the government should propose the continuation of the death penalty, not its elimination. In short, it is evident that the government's attitude to the death penalty in the three six-year periods to which I have referred has allowed the murder rate to rise. Ordinarily, you would think that a minister would say, "I have looked at the figures and think for the time being the death penalty should continue." But for reasons which I do not understand, the minister says exactly the opposite.
I have referred to the attitude of the solicitor general of the United States who made known his views on the death penalty in a brief submitted to the supreme court of the United States. As you know, the United States supreme court has held that the death penalty, in certain circumstances, is constitutional and may be imposed. Many attorneys general of states of the United States hold similar views. They think the death penalty is a deterrent, are fighting to have it instituted in cases where it is not on the statute books and to have it retained in cases where it is.
The attorney general of California, E. J. Younger, submitted two briefs to the United States supreme court. I invite hon. members to read those briefs. In them he set out clearly why it is thought in California that the death penalty is a deterrent. For example, in one brief he says that the Los Angeles police department conducted a survey between December 21, 1970, and February 4, 1971. It interviewed 316 arrestees. Unarmed suspects were asked why they did not arm themselves, and armed suspects who did not use their weapons were asked why they did not. Of the 316 persons interviewed, 217 denied their crime or refused to make a statement, primarily out of a desire not to jeopardize their case. The positive statements made by the remaining 99 are classified as follows:
1.	Deterred by fear of death penalty from carrying weapon or operating weapon, 50 (50.5 per cent).
2.	Unaffected by death penalty because it was no longer being enforced, 7 (7.07 per cent).
3.	Undeterred by death penalty, would kill whether it was enforced or not, 10 (10.1 per cent).
4.	Unaffected by death penalty because they would not carry weapon in any event, primarily out of fear of being injured themselves or of injuring someone else, 32 (32.3 per cent).
Clearly, the majority of those who made statements agreed that they did not carry a weapon because they were frightened of the death penalty. I suggest that even if only one person is deterred from carrying a weapon and committing murder, the death penalty should be retained as a worth-while measure. The attorney general of California stated in his brief:
The conclusions drawn from the study are as follows:
The adoption of an effectively enforced death penalty system is a deterrent in the prevention of homicides.
The report also notes:
If this study contained only one and not the 50 documented cases supporting the fact that the death penalty is a deterrent, there should be no question of its retention and enforcement-
Appendix C to the brief quotes the actual statements made by people who had been arrested. The reasons given for using or not using a weapon are most interesting. For example, one suspect said:
Since in reality there is no death penalty in California, I would kill to obtain what I want.

That was the statement of an unarmed robber. A suspect charged with armed robbery said:
I used a pellet gun because I didn't want to kill anyone and be put to death in the gas chamber.
An unarmed burglar who was charged said:
I don't carry a gun. I don't want to be shot at by police and am afraid of the death penalty.
Another man interviewed who had been charged with armed robbery said:
I used an unloaded gun in the robbery of a market so I would not hurt anyone and because I am afraid of the death penalty.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to ask the unanimous consent of the House to deal with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that all signs indicate that unemployment among students this summer will be even higher than last year's level, which was 14.4 per cent; in view of the fact that the government is directly responsible for much of this unemployment because of its withdrawal of the Opportunities for Youth program, the lack of which departmental studies indicate could have raised student unemployment by two or three per cent last year, and in view of the fact that present Canada student loan plan regulations do not use the amount a student earns during the summer to gauge how much he should be eligible to borrow but instead examine only the number of weeks during which the student was available for work, a procedure which, if followed this fall, will force students unable to find work this summer to discontinue their post-secondary education, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the government of Canada follow the example of the Province of Nova Scotia in dealing with students by basing eligibility for loans on their actual income as defined by the Income Tax Act rather than on the number of weeks they are available for work but are possibly unable to find it.
