subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and motion No. 13 (Mr. Reynolds).

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before lunch I was about to conclude my remarks in support of motion No. 13, and outlining my reasons for hoping that this will be the view taken by the House generally. I was pointing out that there was considerable evidence that the retention of the death penalty would be a deterrent to murder, and to that end I was reading certain relevant parts of a submission made by the attorney general of California to the supreme court of the United States.
In Los Angeles, the police department interviewed various people who had been arrested for certain offences and asked them, for example, why they did not carry a gun or, if they did, why they did not use the gun, and so on. It is interesting to note the number of occasions on which those who had been arrested said they did not carry a gun or resort to the use of a gun because they were afraid of the death penalty. I drew attention to the words of a man charged with armed robbery who said:
I was afraid to use a gun because of a possible death sentence.
Another stated:
I did not use a gun because I am afraid of the death penalty.
Another told the police:
I never owned a gun because I am afraid of the death penalty.
I could go on and call attention to some 25 such comments. When the Solicitor General suggests it has never been proven either way whether the death penalty is a deterrent or not, he is bound to admit that though this may be so, there is strong evidence to show that it is a deterrent. I believe it can be shown that it is a deterrent to murder, particularly of a prison guard or a policeman, and that it would be in the interest of all Canadians if the death penalty for such an offence was retained.
While we torment ourselves over the question of execution, it should not be forgotten that although 11 persons are now in so-called death row-65 people were convicted of murder in the 12 years ending 1974-over 4,000 people have been illegally executed in this country in the course of the crime referred to as murder. Surely this is an equation we have to weigh. More than 4,000 people were illegally executed, or murdered, yet we hesitate to execute legally even the small number to whom I have referred-the 65 persons in the last 12 years who have been charged with murder and sentenced to death.
It is particularly important that we give this protection of a deterrent to those who are upholding our laws, that is to say, our prison guards and policemen. They, after all, are in the front line. They are the people who must deal with convicts and bring offenders to justice. We owe these men an assurance that if any one of them is murdered, his
July 8, 1976

assailant will in turn pay with his life. If we fail to do this, we have let down our policemen and prison guards. That is why I urge hon. members seriously to consider the merits of motion No. 13.
I would point out, also, that if under the present proposal a man who has been convicted of murdering a prison guard or policeman is sentenced to life imprisonment, it does not mean he will spend 25 years in prison. From the day he is put in jail he becomes eligible to get what is called leave of absence, with an escort, at any time. He is able to get that privilege by permission of the jailer or of the Commissioner of Penitentiaries. I believe this provision is unduly lax. I believe it is irresponsible for the government to be suggesting that a hardened criminal, a man convicted of murdering a prison guard or a policeman, should be allowed leave of absence from time to time, with an escort, bearing in mind that it would be easy for one of these hardened criminals to jump his guard and commit another murder.
That is the basis for my belief that hon. members should support motion 13. It is not enough for members on the government side to cite certain people who happen to be abolitionists or retentionists. I think they belie the free vote their Prime Minister claims is in existence every time they make these statements. We in the Conservative caucus believe this is in truth a free vote and that people should decide for themselves how we should dispose of each of these amendments and the bill itself. Every time a government member calls into ridicule, if you like, one of our members who has chosen to vote one way or the other, he is belying the free vote the Prime Minister claims to be in existence.
When speaking of the free vote I would point out that it is time members of this House reflected, in the free vote, the free opinion of Canadians. Canadians wish the death penalty to be retained. I think the time has come when we in this, hopefully, democratic institution should cease to frustrate the free will of Canadians, at least in the case of prison guards and policemen, by allowing the death penalty to be retained.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read very carefully the speeches delivered during the past few days, including of course those of my colleagues of the Social Credit Party, on the proposed amendments to Bill C-84. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just resumed his seat has asked hon. members to vote conscientiously, according to the wishes of their constituents. I am greatly pleased to be the representative of my electors in Parliament. Since the introduction of Bill C-84, we have received hundreds even thousands of letters from all parts of Canada in which people state their views on the abolition of the death penalty.
I think I can truthfully say that at least 90 per cent of the population across Canada, out west, in the east, the Maritimes or the centre, 90 per cent of the people want to retain capital punishment. Now, Motion No. 13 before us advocates the retention of capital punishment for the murder of policemen and prison guards. Mr. Speaker, I believe that policemen and prison guards have made
Capital Punishment
representations to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) as well as to the Prime Minister, the cabinet and all federal representatives.
On June 22 last, we voted on second reading on Bill C-84 which was defeated. The vote upheld Bill C-84 by 133 votes against 125. What happened to me may have happened to other members or other political parties. On June 22, the vote was taken at noon. At two o'clock in the afternoon, I was returning home to Rouyn by car, and in the evening, around 7 or 7:30, at my Hull residence, a carpenter was doing some repair work. A blue car stopped at my place and the driver, a chap of 25 or 26, called the carpenter to his car and asked him: Where is Caouette, the guy in favour of hanging; I want to kill him! As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, this chap had a revolver next to him on the front seat of the car, and was ready to kill a member who had voted for capital punishment for murderers. But then, the protection we would need, no member has it presently. I know full well that those individuals, either in Montreal, here in Ottawa or in Hull, as it happened at my place, have set for themselves or have been assigned the task of trying to influence the members or to frighten them by threatening them with death if they vote for the retention of capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, when in a system or a country like ours we have reached the point where we have to put up with or tolerate that sort of people, I think the members should think twice before deciding: For all practical purposes, we are going to abolish capital punishment in Canada, even for murderers of policemen, prison guards, my wife, my children, the wives and children of everyone, even members of parliament, the Prime Minister and the other ministers. We should have protection against those people! Of course not, there is an attempt to frighten people, and that is when I wonder how true is the free vote on capital punishment in this House.
I said before June 22 that I was in favour of capital punishment for qualified gangsters, and I say it again today: capital punishment must be urgently restored in Canada, not as a revenge against anyone, but so justice will prevail for all the public, for Canadians, for our families, for government leaders, authorities, everybody.
Mr. Speaker, when we reach a point where we have contract killers, people paid to go and kill someone, we are going to arrest those people, we are going to locate them, we are going to sentence them to 25 years in prison and they are going to cost us maybe $20,000 or $25,000 a year for subsistance, and we are going to keep those individuals under the pretext that we can rehabilitate them. Mr. Speaker, I am anxious to see the Solicitor General try and rehabilitate just one of those notorious gangsters who have only one reason to live, to commit murders and kill their fellow men.
Mr. Speaker, recently the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who supports the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) on capital punishment, said that in the name of humanity, we have no right to kill a criminal, even if he has killed a guard, a policeman or anybody else, we have no right to send him off to the guillotine or to the noose because it does not bring back the victim to life nor does it rehabili-

July 8, 1976
Capital Punishment
tate the criminal. Mr. Speaker, everybody knows that, we did not need a prime minister or a solicitor general to tell us that. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is not here, but I hope he will read my comments. Recently, the Prime Minister took a little trip to Cuba, he told us how beautiful it was, how Mr. Castro runs the country well, that Mr. Castro was a very humane man. But, Mr. Speaker, I ask the Prime Minister of Canada to send terrorists to Cuba, well-known criminals, to do there what they do in Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa or Hull. How long would Mr. Castro tolerate them in Cuba? Precisely in the name of humanitarianism and humanity, in the name of the right to life, how long would those people live in the country known as Cuba, under the regime of Mr. Castro, a close friend of the Prime Minister of Canada?
Mr. Speaker, everyone knows the answer to that question. A bandit would not live two hours. Why? Because we know that what used to be past practise in that country is no longer tolerated. When Mr. Castro was a revolutionary, a terrorist, he was tolerated by the authorities of the day. The moment he took power in Cuba, he got rid of officials, lowly civil servants, people by the thousands. Pits were dug by bulldozers with special blades and people were lined up along the pits. Then, they were fired upon so that they would fall, dead, into the holes, on Mr. Castro's orders.
The Prime Minister did not tell us that when he came back from Cuba. He does not speak of that when he introduces or has the Solicitor General of Canada introduce Bill C-84. What group in our Canadian society asked that this bill to be introduced in the House? What part of Canada asked the Solicitor General or the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada or the Liberal government to introduce Bill C-84 to abolish capital punishment in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I know that some hon. members are now under extreme pressure in their constituencies that they are being harassed from all sides by their electors who are against abolishing capital punishment. But no, they come here and they say that perhaps they will be able to restore their popularity before the next election. They vote against and we say: we vote according to our conscience.

Even the 10 per cent do not speak as loudly as all that, but the 90 per cent do not mince their words when talking about punishments which bandits and hardened criminals deserve; we do not clamour for hanging as we knew it 25 or 30 years ago, but it is as clear as crystal that in the case of premeditated murder, someone wanted to kill someone.
Then, let us try to rehabilitate such a bandit or murderer; I challenge the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) to rehabilitate only one across Canada and in the province of Quebec. In his own riding, the Solicitor General has a vast majority of retentionists. The same applies to the right hon. Prime Minister. I mentioned earlier all those countries, I talked about Cuba, but there are other countries in the world. Let us talk about murderers in the U.S.S.R. for instance. Recently, a Russian businessman was conducting financial transactions with Swiss financiers. The Soviet government found him out. They did not charge him with murder; he was told that he has worked against the state and he was shot the next morning. Would terrorists be tolerated in Russia? Those who were in power in 1916, 1917, 1918 and 1919 were terrorists. With Lenin and Marx first, and then with Stalin. Does the Prime Minister stand to protest against massive executions that are taking place in the U.S.S.R., in Czechoslovakia, in Poland, in the whole communist block? The same is happening there. In other areas of the world which are not cummunist, in Africa, in Morocco, one day not too long ago 17 individuals were shot because of their revolting against a government bill.
In these countries, which are said to be as civilized as we are capital punishment exists for murders far less sordid than those that have happened in Montreal for too many years now. Recently, an aircraft was hijacked by pirates who flew to Uganda. We saw how this one ended not too long ago: about thirty dead. These people would be alive if there had not been any pirates, but there were and they were prepared to kill 106 hostages in an aircraft which did not belong to them. These pirates are dead now. But if they had not been shot and had come to Canada, we would have sued them and said: Gentlemen, there might be a way to
July 8, 1976

rehabilitate you. We will send you to prison for 20 or 25 years for life, but maybe you will stay only 15 or 10 years depending on the application, on the way the judge feels. Then you might be released in 10, 12 or 15 years.
Then, they had the right to shoot down the leaders of the hijackers. As for the policemen, the prison guards, since they expect some security, will we allow them greater latitude in return, will we let them defend themselves effectively and efficiently through Bill C-84? No, we still want to control their actions, to expose them to the bandits, the prisoners, the convicts in isolation who are ready to do anything in order to escape and commit the same odious crime.
Mr. Speaker, why are our policemen and our prison guards so shocked and so much against Bill C-84? Their security is at stake. When a policeman of about 24 or 25 arrests a bandit, charges him and proves that he is a bandit, this young policeman sees the bandit or the murderer condemned to 15 or 20 years in prison. Do you know that 15 years from now this criminal who is only 25 years old will be only 40, no more than that. At that time, he will be freed. Do you not think he will rather resent his 10 or 15 years in prison? At that time, he will be incited to settle with the policeman who arrested him when he was 25.
Mr. Speaker, I find absolutely illogical that supposedly reasonable people ask us and advocate across the board abolition of the death penalty in Canada. As I said earlier, we receive hundreds of letters from people protesting against the abolition of the death penalty and not only from people in the province of Quebec. One of these letters has been sent to me by a Mr. Lessard who lives on Henri-Bourassa West in Montreal. He simply sent me a few words to tell me:
I hope that, in Parliament, you are going to help us so that the death penalty will not be abolished.
Raynald Lessard, Montreal.
Some people ask that the death penalty be maintained, not for revenge but in a spirit of justice. As I said the last time I spoke in the House on this subject: There are traffic laws. I consider the death penalty as a warning to everyone: Do not kill your fellow being, or it will be dangerous for you. A red light at the corner of the street. What does that mean? Stop! Mr. Speaker, you are free not to stop but, if you do not stop, you might create a serious accident which could claim several lives. Mr. Speaker, at that moment, a man is free but the signal says: Stop. The law asks him to stop. I see the penalty in exactly the same way, it is a stop signal: Stop, do not kill your fellow being because if you do kill him you will bear the consequences of your act. That is what murderers should be told throughout Canada.
Mr. Speaker, those people know it. If we say to them: Listen, the noose is there. I do not want to hang anybody but neither do I want anybody to kill his fellow being. In this case, he will not risk hanging. I am not afraid to be hanged because I know that I have not killed anyone and I do not intend to kill anyone either. But when you see that there are people who steal, people who are contract killers and who are paid to kill, let us not imagine that I am going to believe that these people are fully repentant and have decided never to do it again when they are paid so much a head, so much per murder. Mr. Speaker, I do not trust these

people and besides they do not frighten me. I am not afraid to tell them to their face what I think of those who are killers, these human monsters of our so-called civilized society. Mr. Speaker, I have other letters and this one from Toronto says this:
It was like a breath of fresh air to read that you and all members of your party solidly voted for the retention of capital punishment and it proved to all Canadians across Canada that you and your party was the only political party that was listening to the voice of the public to retain capital punishment.

All our members of the Social Credit Party.
I have noticed, Mr. Speaker, that some members of the Liberal Party voted for retention of capital punishment, according to the views of thier constituents. I have noticed also that many Progressive Conservatives voted for retention of capital punishment. And I have noticed that among the members of the New Democratic Party-

The letter from Toronto which I am quoting goes on as follows:

In view of the fact that the leaders of the other parties, such as Trudeau, Clark and Broadbent and the majority of their MPs ignored the desire of the voters to retain capital punishment, their actions on this critical issue will certainly cost them a loss of voters and MPs will suffer with the loss of their seats at the next election-
The letter was written by P. Bennett, of Toronto, on June 30, 1976.

Mr. Speaker, it is a Mr. Bennett, B-e-n-n-e-t-t, from Toronto, June 30. I did not request anything from him. I suggested some months ago to the Prime Minister that this stand on capital punishment was flying in the face of people in Montreal, Quebec, Vancouver and Toronto. That might be the issue that would cause the defeat of this Liberal government at the next election, either in one or two years. I am still of that opinion. The Canadian people has seen enough of a government that goes against their will, against their wishes, against their stated desires.
Here is another letter, from Ottawa:

What else can I say? Congratulations, but a poor result, 133 to 125. I am very pleased to see that your party MPs voted for hanging and it may pay off in the next federal election.

I am not counting on that, but I feel that all my colleagues in the Social Credit and myself voted according to the wishes not only of Quebecers, but of Canadians as a whole. Some Progressive Conservative and Liberal members know that. The New Democrats are insensitive, they are unaware of it.
Mr. Speaker, I have here a letter received from Residence Dorchester, in Montreal, 1650 W. Dorchester Blvd. Mr. Lucien Roussel writes:
The abolition of capital punishment by our federal government is not fair.
Following that decision, I would agree if at the next federal election we were asked on every ballot: Are you in favour of capital punishment or not?
This is a man who suggests that a referendum be held. We talked about the referendum. I already suggested it to the Solicitor General, the right hon. Prime Minister, this government, this House. They are afraid to let the people speak up, and all those who held some kind of referendum in their respective ridings received similar answers. From 85 to 90 per cent answered this: Retain capital punishment for capital murders, premeditated murders, not only for
murderers of policemen and prison guards but for all murderers. That is what those people are suggesting-a referendum. The Prime Minister tells us, no, no, no referendum.
The Solicitor General also tells us, no, no, no referendum. That is because he knows he would be beaten. That is why I keep asking who else has asked this government to bring Bill C-84 before the House? Who? What part of Canada? What member? What association? Would the murderers themselves have asked this government, please spare us the noose, we will be good little boys, so keep on protecting us. That is exactly what Bill C-84 does. It protects bandits against society instead of protecting society against bandits and criminals.
Mr. Speaker, I have here another letter from Montreal, from Mr. Bernard Molloy who says:
Congratulations on the stand you and your party took with regard to capital punishment. You are to be admired for having the courage of your convictions.

Mr. Speaker, this is the type of letters I get, but I did not receive a single one in favour of abolition. Is it because abolitionist are afraid to write to me? Not a single one! I got some against abolition from all parts of Canada, even the Yukon and the Northwest Territories.
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the Social Credit Party is not the only one who receives letters; others do too. My colleagues receive a lot of them and there is a general outcry for the retention of capital punishment, and I repeat, it is not in a spirit of vengence but in a spirit of justice. Let justice be done, rendered and obtained. Instead of thinking of the rehabilition of such bandits, let us think about their victims and their families. When a manager of a Caisse populaire with his child in his arms is killed in cold blood and shot point-blank, when that chap entered the house to rob with a loaded revolver, well, he did not go in with his rosary to do the stations of the Cross.
He went in there firmly decided to shoot if things turned out bad. Mr. Speaker, this is precisely what happened. The father, the wife, a mother of a family, were killed. Recently in Montreal, we have witnessed I think the fifty-second qualified murder in the City of Montreal alone, in the MUC. And the same thing happens in the Quebec City region and in the region of Trois-Rivieres. The same holds true for Toronto as well as Vancouver.
Mr. Speaker, I think that motion No. 13 which aims at protecting policemen and prison guards must be agreed to by the House. I have noticed some hon. members who rose and were not afraid to vote on second reading. I congratulate them for that. As for those who were prompted by fear, who voted to avoid that this government be defeated, their case is a bit more doubtful and I say to them: You will have it out with your constituents. Meanwhile, let us think about the people of Canada who deserve to be protected, who deserve an assurance from a government that their life is being protected against gangsters, criminals, murderers, genuine and hardened criminals, those who cannot be rehabilitated.

July 8, 1976

If we secured the protection of policemen and prison guards, we would at least make a move in a direction where we might reach if not perfection at least a better safety than we now enjoy. For that purpose, I am still in favour of capital punishment, not against occasional criminals but for hardened criminals, those who have revengeful and hateful feelings for their fellow citizens or society as a whole.
Let us improve living conditions within society. I agree, if this means preventing some people from going wrong; however, I think it would cost less than maintaining criminals in our jails. If we gave them more respectable, more affordable living conditions finally to prevent those who have still some good in them from committing murder. Let us prepare ourselves before it is too late, but if society, government and the law are to be abused then let the murderer pay for his crime.

Mr. Speaker, we are discussing two amendments today. They have been joined together because they both refer to clause 4 of this bill. I was delighted to hear that in the last two or three days the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) indicated that he is prepared to accept the amendment proposed by my colleague and friend, the hon. member for Northumber-land-Durham (Mr. Lawrence).
I will not address myself to that particular amendment because my concern is mainly with a statement made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) which appears in yesterday's Hansard. In that statement there was an unusual development of thought which I find difficult to understand. I thought I would use my intervention this afternoon to describe what an unusual position the hon. member has got himself into by using the logic he did. The anomalous situation into which he has talked himself is manifest in two clearly distinguishable respects. I cannot understand how he arrived at his conclusion. There may be some explanation and we may go into that afterwards. But we must remember that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is a self-declared retentionist, and I am glad of that. I am a retentionist myself. Also, on second reading the hon. member voted with the retentionists.
The hon. member declared, in a statement which appears at page 15133 of Hansard, that he believes in the retention of capital punishment. That is fine.

In other words, he

wanted return to the law as it now stands, because he is a retentionist. However, the hon. member is opposed to the present amendment which would reinstate the death penalty.

And the law as it is, although, granted, only to this extent. Why is he opposed to this amendment? He says it is because it introduces discrimination. The existing law is discriminatory, but the hon. member cannot go beyond that because backbenchers on this side or on the side opposite cannot extend the intent of the law as it now stands. That is the prerogative of the government. The extent to which the present law is discriminatory seems to have been what the hon. member voted for in the first instance. The second reason he has placed himself in this untenable position by his unusual stand is that he seems completely unaware of the fact that he could accomplish his purpose as a retentionist by supporting this amendment. It is as simple as that.
In my cogitations, if this amendment is carried it stands to reason the government will have to withdraw the bill. If the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) is approved in the vote tonight, the bill will be completely demolished and it will have to be withdrawn or rewritten. It would have to be presented again-and I have no doubt that it would be- but that is the situation and the purpose of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni would be accomplished for the time being, anyway. Is he a bellwether just giving an indication to the rest of the retentionists in this chamber that this is the way the backbenchers on the government side are going to vote? I am not sure of that, although it may be a possibility. I hope he will reconsider his position, and having reconsidered it will alter the way he intends to vote when the time comes tonight. I will not point the finger and say, "You have changed your mind"; no, sir. That hon. member can change his mind because he will see that he will be accomplishing his purpose if he votes tonight in favour of this amendment.
There are other aspects of the amendment on which I feel I must comment. Last weekend I was at a July 1 ceremony in a small community in my riding and I heard a story which upset me very deeply. This came to me from someone who had been talking to the RCMP, which is the police force responsible for enforcing the law in that community of 5,000 or 6,000 people. I was told that in that apparently law-abiding community where there is a detachment of three, four or five policemen, at least once a month, when in pursuit of their duty and on patrol, they stare down the operative end of a gun barrel. That is a frightening thought, in a community which I have the honour to represent, that once a month these men are faced with a weapon that could go off.
Let us not forget that police, prison guards, penitentiary workers and those listed in section 214 of the Criminal Code, such as sherriff's officers and prison employees engaged in the preservation and maintenance of public institutions, and so on, are all public servants. They are the only civilian public servants whose lives we have been
95570-591/2

July 8, 1976
Capital Punishment
prepared to place at great risk, Mr. Speaker. 1 have just mentioned one of the risks these public servants have to face.
I would ask the government what plans it has to protect these public servants if this bill should pass. Most of them are married and have families. If the breadwinner happens to be a victim in the commission of a crime, what provision does the government make, over and above the ordinary provision that is now made by the public service, for this particular class of public servant? If there is a pension or superannuation plan, is the government going to demand extra premiums from them so that they can pay for taking these extra risks, or is the government going to provide the extra premium and the benefits that would be required by these public servants? These are matters that obviously have not been thought of, so far as I can make out.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the federal government could do this, but what about the provinces and the municipalities who also have public servants who are at great risk, some of whom might lose their lives? The risk is going to be greater if this bill should pass. Many more of these public servants, let us be frank, will pay with their lives. What about their survivors? What means does the government have to offer in order to entice, to induce or to recruit properly qualified persons to fill these risk positions? I do not think they have any particular plans in mind. These public servants are our protectors. They stand between us and the criminals in our society who have decided that they can disregard the law.
I do not think the government has looked ahead to see what the response of some of our policemen is likely to be when dealing with serious crimes. With the threat of the death penalty eliminated by the successful passage of this bill, when they are dealing with crimes involving the killing of policemen, who amongst us, would blame a guardian of the law who decided to use his sidearm first in the apprehension of a dangerous criminal? Who would be to blame if we were to find that the death penalty was carried out not infrequently before trial? Is this what we want?

This is not just a remote possibility, Mr. Speaker. In raising the matter I do not question the integrity, self-control and discipline of our police forces. Wherever I have met them they have given me cause to be proud. But self-defence would be a justifiable defence in most of the circumstances that one can envisage. Is that what the government wants-execution without trial, to avoid execution upon conviction? That is what it looks like.
I therefore propose, even in this limited context, to support the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta which will give policemen and others who work for our protection, at least some protection rather than have them face the dreadful decision of having to shoot first and ask questions afterwards.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a few of my thoughts before the House and say at the outset that I support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds). In the days since the vote was taken on second reading of this bill a number of members who voted for abolition in the almost cocoon-like security of this place have possibly been faced with the stark reality of what their constituents were saying when they went back to their ridings. Some who thought that the figure of 80 per cent of Canadians endorsing the retention of capital punishment for premeditated murder was an exaggeration possibly found that 80 per cent was on the low side when they returned to their ridings.
I have to go back to 1972, Mr. Speaker. To all intents and purposes the amendment before us restores the law to the position it is in at the moment. Capital punishment would be the penalty for the murder of police officers or prison guards. I recall that in 1972 the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), an avowed abolitionist, said in an interview that he would have liked to go for complete abolition but this was the best he could get at the time. There was a minority government in 1972-73, and to my mind he had no intention of enforcing the bill that he proposed to this House. He was convinced that in every case to come before him he would try to convince the cabinet to commute the death penalty called for in the law which he sponsored.
The facts cannot be gainsaid. I submit that the death penalty should be maintained for the murderers of police officers and prison guards. Right now some prison guards are opting for early retirement. Many of them are veterans who took up their duties with the prison service at the end of World War II. Many have served 25 years. They need 30 years' service for a full pension, and quite a number are opting for early retirement. Why is that, Mr. Speaker? They seriously question the policies of the Solicitor General, the minister responsible for our prison service. They wonder if he has listened to their pleas. They are concerned not only about capital punishment; they are concerned about the whole question of security in prisons and say, "We do not have the support of the Solicitor General. Has he even listened to us?" Therefore, some of them are opting for early retirement. The situation in provincial jail systems is similar. Even now the Manitoba government is embarking on a plan whereby it will recruit officers to serve in Manitoba jails in future.
I know that last weekend many members did as I did; I visited the various parts of my riding and spoke to many people about capital punishment. Actually, it is more accurate to say that they spoke to me about capital punishment. There was no way to avoid them. They wanted to speak about it. I had the chance to speak with some RCMP personnel in my riding. I can best describe their attitude by saying they are angry, frustrated and, above all, cynical. They have become cynical about the government. You can tell them that the vote on the bill is free, but they know it is a government-supported bill, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Solicitor General, avowed abolitionists, wanted to bring this before the House for passage before the end of the last five-year experiemental period.
It is known that this bill has been brought before the House despite the objections of the vast majority of Canadians who hold retentionist views with regard to premeditated murder. RCMP officers legitimately ask, as do prison guards, how they are to act. Obviously, there is a

July 8, 1976

communications gap between the RCMP and the Solicitor General, the minister who is supposedly responsible for the force and who does not listen. He does not do what the RCMP recommends. A police organization in Calgary says it cannot place any trust in the Solicitor General, a position also adopted by some members of the RCMP.
It was put this way to me, and I emphasize that I am not alluding to a contrived or unrealistic situation, because what I am about to mention could happen, "How is an RCMP officer to act, once this bill passes, if he faces a gunman with a loaded gun?" Let us say the gunman has already killed an innocent victim who is not a police officer or prison guard. The RCMP are called in to apprehend that person; they arrive at the scene and find themselves looking down the barrel of a high-powered rifle. What are they to do? In that situation you do not use polite language and say, "Please put down your gun and come with me." Gunmen do not understand such language. Therefore, because a policeman must act in self-defence it is possible that the gunman will be shot and killed. Will the RCMP be accused by abolitionists, including the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General, of taking the law into their own hands, of setting up a kangaroo court, acting as judge and jury and, instead of arresting him, shooting the gunman down?
Some may say that argument is strained, that the situation is contrived. I submit they are wrong. The RCMP do not think that situation is far-fetched. Right now they could face similar situations almost every day of the week. They ask, if they are forced to act in the manner described, who will defend them? Will it be the Solicitor General in whom they have no faith? They have received no answer to that question. I submit that the Solicitor General is obliged to answer. Be that as it may, our policemen will face gunmen and the situation I have described is not contrived. Therefore, fundamental questions remain to be answered.
Today our police forces are cynical. Society is cynical. It feels that parliament defied the will of the majority of Canadians by voting for abolition. I suppose all members of parliament wonder how best to ascertain the opinion of those they represent. I do not know how other members operate, but speaking for myself I often phone the same people to learn their opinions. Unfortunately, this procedure is not always satisfactory. To ascertain more accurately the views of people in the riding with respect to the retention of capital punishment for premeditated murder, I found it necessary to conduct a poll. The poll showed that the majority of my constituents are in favour of retention. I suggest that in no constituency is the majority of constituents in favour of abolition. If that were the case we would have heard about it a long time ago. One would have heard abolitionist members saying, "The majority of constituents in my riding favour abolition." They have not said that; on that point they have been remarkably silent. One can only conclude that such sentiment does not exist.
When I spoke on second reading I made my position as a retentionist well known and told the House that I had conducted a poll with respect to Bill C-84. Mr. Speaker, 90 per cent of the respondents in my riding opted for the retention of capital punishment for premeditated murder. I am not a professional pollster and my poll may not have
Capital Punishment
been conducted scientifically. But even if you reduce the percentage in favour by 10 per cent, from 90 per cent to 80 per cent, you still wind up with an overwhelming majority, with a virtual consensus. That is how the people of my riding feel. I suggest that the poll results pertaining to my riding are not unique but hold true to a lesser or greater degree in every riding across Canada.
It is not only police and prison officials who are cynical and frustrated. Canadians are frustrated as well. They are questioning whether the representations they have made have been listened to. We have in this motion the retention of capital punishment for the killing of police officers or prison guards. Police associations and policemen's wives associations have indicated their position to us. They live under constant fear because of the risks inherent in their jobs. They have indicated that their fear is intensified because there is no longer the ultimate deterrent. Even though death sentences have been commuted since 1962, there has always been the possibility that a person convicted of murder would in fact pay the supreme penalty.
An example of the deterrent value was clearly brought out in the Israeli raid. I know that treason and hijacking were discussed earlier. However, one of my constituents pointed out that if capital punishment had been in force, and enforced in the countries where the terrorists were incarcerated, they could not have been used as ransom for the lives of those hijackers held on the Air France plane.
Whether we like to admit it or not, police officers and prison guards are being asked to put their lives on the line, with even less protection. Abolitionists are willing to accept those additional risks. They are willing to accept the death of these people because it is inherent in their jobs. I can interpret the view of the abolitionists in no other way. They are quite willing to extend those risks to the point where police officers and prison guards will have to sacrifice their lives, rather than retain the death penalty as at least a measure of protection for a person who is innocent. Innocent people are being asked to put their lives on the line in order to protect those who have already taken a life. That is not in any way compatible with justice.
The major question still facing me on the whole capital punishment issue is that some people say that if we invoke capital punishment, rehabilitation is impossible. From what I have seen, I do not believe that rehabilitation through the prison system works. I know we have had experts of all types in there, including psychiatrists, psychologists, and so on. I do not say this because I am a pessimist. I would love to see rehabilitation take effect. However, the state, by its very nature, does not have the ability to rehabilitate people. The state is impersonal, it depersonalizes everything. We have seen this happen in prisons. The state has no heart.
The only rehabilitation that will take place is in cases where organizations and individuals are willing to work with prisoners in a slow, ongoing process. A person might then be rehabilitated to the degree where he or she accepts the laws of the country, obeys those laws, and recognizes that by breaking a law the very basis of democracy is threatened because democracy can only survive if he or she

July 8, 1976
Capital Punishment
respects the rights of others. However, killers take away the basic right of individuals, and that is life.
There are idealists in this House who say that if we do not have capital punishment for premeditated killers, we can work on rehabilitation. The Solicitor General will have to be the first to admit that rehabilitation in our prisons has been a disaster.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, motion No. 13 which we are now studying is, to my mind, one of the most important motions that have been presented and which is on the order paper of the House in respect of Bill C-84. Indeed, this amendment, motion No. 13, proposes to maintain present Criminal Code section 214 or to delete clause 4 of the bill.
It is not without reason, I think, that many people, organizations and policemen throughout Canada are opposed to the deletion of section 214.
I am satisfied that each member studies carefully this question at the moment. We are studying together what we should do to give society, individuals and families the protection they are entitled to. We want to reach that aim by different means but, nevertheless, I think we must take into account the representations which are made to us and also the fact that policemen are friends of society.
In the past, policemen were often considered as persons to fear, persons that we should not get in touch with. They were not considered as friends. They were considered as people who had the authority to punish. It was in some ways the mentality that prevailed among the population. Fortunately, that mentality has changed. More and more the youth consider policemen as persons that should be
July 8, 1976

respected because they wield authority. They have the authority, they have been given a mandate to make people respect the laws adopted by parliaments. Therefore, policemen do not simply have the mission to punish; they also have the mission to enforce the law and protect the life and the property of individuals. The greatest proof of that is that when our rights are threatened by bandits, we call on policemen. When we are threatened by people who do not respect the rights and the property of others, we once again call on the police for protection.
If we ask for their protection, we parliamentarians have the obligation to ensure the protection of policemen as well, to place in their hands the weapons to accomplish their mission, and I am not talking about a gun or a revolver because we all know that this is necessary, but I want to say that policemen should be ensured by society that if they lose their life in the course of their duties against those who do not want to obey the law, an example would be made for the benefit of others who would be tempted to do the same. Murderers must be punished. This is what Criminal Code section 214 provides. And this is why I have no hesitation in supporting motion No. 13 because it aims at maintaining in our statutes some protection for our policemen, prison guards, all those employees who work in prisons, who are responsible for guarding and controlling prisoners, so that they may have the required protection, just like we now require on building sites that contractors take all the necessary precautions to prevent accidents to their workers. For instance, wearing a hard hat, using a cable when a roof is too steep, wearing a safety belt, all of which aim at protecting the life of workers. Therefore, the employees who work in prison or the policemen who work on the road are entitled to the same protection.
However, I believe that the question we must consider during the study of this bill is why are we now living in a violent society and why are many individuals now thinking that they must make their own justice. We hear this often nowadays. We say it, we hear it, but there is no order anymore. We are living in a violent society. We are never sure when we go out to the grocery store if we shall come back alive. Therefore, people think of making their own justice.
This is not a healthy society: indeed, the society is ill: it is a society in which there is violence. What are the causes? I think that television, movies and theatres are the main causes of violence. Violence does not exist only in Canada, it exists also elsewhere. But it is also where there is television, movies and theatres where so many things incite to violence.
It is deplorable to find that in Canada, our children are being shown violent films for hours at a time, and that happens every day. They are taught violence, the use of firearms, how to attack people, how to make a hold up, all kinds of violent ways. And our young people are looking at these for hours, and then, in their mind projects develop, so that at a given moment, faced with an economic situation rather difficult in the family, some young people will consider using these means, these weapons, they will take violent action to get a few dollars to do what they please. That is called teaching crime. People were shocked in old
Capital Punishment
times when the Romans made a show of death in the eyes of the public. People were shocked by that and we are also shocked when we read about it. That was done in the arena, just like cock-fighting today. In the end, one of them dies.
Today, it is not done on the stage, it is not done in the same fashion, but through images. Our children are given to see on television all kinds of films inviting to violence and after that we are suprised and wonder what is happening. Young people no longer want to abide by the law, their ideas are different from those of adults and they often cause serious problems in society. If we were in their place, we would perhaps do worse than them, because I think if we had to live in the same atmosphere and had been shown the same things in our young age, we would be even worse. They are not to be blamed; instead we should blame the adults who are responsible for seeing to it that the films shown on television and in cinemas really encourage respect for life, respect for human beings. Those children could still be entertained and shown excellent material, and they would be only too happy to get an education that instills respect for life, for other people's property, and teaches them to use their energy in wholesome entertainment while respecting peace and order.
Mr. Speaker, the League of Human Rights, which puts out a bulletin from which I have an excerpt here that I would like to quote you, is entirely of that opinion. I should like to quote you paragraph 3, on page 6, which says:
The information given by the press with regard to crime, especially as exploited by some groups ... is dealt with in such a way as to spread a collective psychosis of dangerous crime and give the wrong impression.
To my mind, there is truly food for thought in that paragraph. To go back to the quotation:
Contrary to what is being done in other fields, the press is quite content to focus the attention of the public on the most negative aspects, without analyzing them as they often should, while overlooking the positive information related, among other things, to the methods of rehabilitation.
So the negative aspects are exploited with great delight because that is profitable and sensational. But we fail to show the positive side. I continue to quote:
We think the press could help the population give criminality its proper dimensions if certain efforts were made in this direction.
Parliament and parliamentarians are responsible for passing legislation so that news media are forced to show the good side of things, to give positive information. We should stop going from one sensational piece of information to another to increase sales or the interest which can induce people to go and see things they own in order to get rich with these businesses.
On clause 4-The rate of violence in the programs of our television and cinema networks is obviously the reflection of a society which consumes violence excessively, without measuring the impact of this consumption on the making of criminality.
We really get down to rock bottom when expressing ourselves this way. One wonders about the following question:
Should not we directly face that matter?
So they suggest:
Governments, in cooperation with all competent and concerned associations, should establish school and adult education programs which

July 8, 1976
Capital Punishment
would make people ponder over the crime phenomenon and which would be basically oriented towards prevention, information and education.
We especially appeal to teachers and parents for their commitment to fight against the initiation to violence which dominates our society, in all kinds of areas and forms, from the most evident to the slyest.
We believe, among other things, that one of the best means to fight destructive violence is the initiation to positive forms of respect for life, which can be found massively and constantly in the various functions inherent in education.
Whatever measures are taken to fight murder and the most dangerous forms of crime directly, they may prove useless if there is not in Quebec and across Canada a systematic and general effort by the public to substitute patterns of human development for the countless violent patterns generated by our society. There again, we think that the most powerful weapons will come from our investing into social values, to really ensure respect for life and the emphasis of what is positive and beautiful in the development of human beings. What good is it to develop all those communication and information techniques if we cannot use them primarily to propagate life?
This was published by the Human Eights Association which sent us this announcement out of which I have quoted a few passages which I heartily support because 1 think this association is working for human rights and that it was duty bound to make its position known on such an important bill.
I said earlier that the economic causes must also be eliminated. I am not the only one to think so, for I believe that those who really think about it are convinced that certain economic causes also lead to violence, crime, and sometimes to revenge or to the temptation to take the lives of those who stand in our way. One can see the turn of mind of such people.
The Chief Justice of the Ontario Supreme Court stated, and I quote:
Canada will begin to control crime only by eliminating the economic needs which, in my opinion, prompt thousands of Canadians to break the law.
Therefore, I think that being a judge, he was able to size all the accused who appeared before him, in order to keep an open mind and to determine why such or such accused appeared before the court. And as a judge, he had to hear the evidence to be able to make a sound judgement.
Then, Mr. Speaker, it will be remembered that policemen have been murdered recently in the province of New Brunswick, that they were inflicted atrocious pains before being slain. Everybody was shocked by such atrocities and following these unfortunate events, policemen from everywhere in Canada got together to ask once more for the retention of capital punishment. All those people cannot be wrong at the same time.
There must certainly be good reasons prompting them to ask parliamentarians to retain capital punishment. That does not necessarily mean hanging. We could use hanging of course but we can take any kind of capital punishment, the most humane so as to respect the concept of the importance of human life and whenever an execution is to be carried out, it should be done as humanely as possible.
I think it must be considered. We shall also recall that last spring, in the Quebec City area, a policeman was killed in cold blood in the course of his duties and here I wish to

quote from an article in the newspaper La Presse of Montreal, of March 3, 1976 entitled:

I wish to quote this article, Mr. Speaker, as I think it is time that as parliamentarians we take into consideration representations made by those who are responsible for protecting the life and property of Canada. I quote:
Some 2,000 policemen gathered in Quebec City after the funeral of one of their colleagues were unanimous. When one of their leaders, the director of the Quebec City section of the provincial policemen association said: "The abolition of capital punishment, never.'', the policemen rose to applaud. And we can easily understand them.
They had come from several areas of the country to express their sorrow after the death of constable Michel Bedard. He died because of his faithfulness to his duties. A criminal, miserable as every criminal, killed him in his escape. This act is so disgusting that it creates revolt and passion. First the policemen offered their sympathy to the close relatives of the deceased at a touching ceremony. Then they got together. And briefly they enounced the principle that should protect them against the madness of killers: "Abolition of capital punishment, never!" We can understand, but are they right?
Mr. Speaker, I will not read this very interesting article in its totality, but once again parliamentarians are asked to do their duty to ensure those people full protection. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, as I realize that the clock runs very fast, I wish to quote two extracts from a booklet published by the Solicitor General of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my English and French-speaking colleagues of the Parliament of Canada for their kindness. As I said, I wish to quote from a booklet published by the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Allmand), in which he says the following in paragraph 6:
6. THE POOR AND MINORITY GROUPS. When capital punishment was in force, it was mostly applied to the poor, non-educated people, minority groups and immigrants. The rich who could afford the best lawyers and were influent had strong chances of being acquitted or getting a reduced sentence.
I know the Solicitor General has much more experience than I do in this area. But when I read that statement, I had doubts about our courts. I often heard people say: There are two justices-one for the rich and one for the poor. But I did not believe that a Crown minister could state it so clearly. Then, in that case, it is again our duty as parliamentarians to see that our laws are the best possible, that they are applied in the fairest way and above all, that judges who are appointed are really qualified, and not selected on the basis of some political patronage but following the recommendation of the Bar because of their knowledge, their occupation, which is really that of protectors of the law and not because of political services rendered.
Mr. Speaker, I would not like to give the impression of accusing judges in any part of Canada or of the province of Quebec, but I wish to take this opportunity to emphasize
July 8, 1976

that if it is true that the poor have fewer chances than the rich to gain justice before the courts, this demonstrates that society is sicker than I thought, and I wish we did our best to take as many steps as possible to put it back in shape at all levels; not only as regards the poor but as regards the rich as well. And if it is true that justice can be influenced to that extent, it becomes outrageous and this is why it is called a society of violence.
We must really ensure that any segment of society, no matter its financial position, when it is faced to courts, be confident before those courts to obtain justice, whether they can or not pay the high price. Again, I hope we will seriously consider this point and that sooner or later the Solicitor General of Canada will be able to introduce amendments to ensure the best protection possible to all citizens as regards law enforcement, when this law must be adhered to by the courts, when someone has been convicted before society.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I again as for the help of all my colleagues in Parliament: For God's sake, tonight will see again the end of a memorable day. An extremely serious vote will take place. I, for one, do not take things lightly because tomorrow and in the days and years to come, everything will depend upon the action we will take tonight. I have no judgment to make about any of my colleagues, be they in favour of or against capital punishment. It is a personal matter, but I think, as the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) said a moment ago, that not only we have the right to vote according to our own conscience but it is our duty to vote according to the people's will.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure you I will be brief, but I should like to put on the record a few thoughts about this amendment. I, like the hon. member for Comox Alberni (Mr. Anderson), do not particularly like this amendment. I am in favour of the retention of capital punishment for premeditated murder and I believe policemen and prison guards need protection. However, I also believe that housewives, children and everyone else in our society need the protection afforded by capital punishment. Having said that I do not like the amendment, I want to assure the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) that I am going to support it since it is perhaps better than complete abolition. It is better to retain the death penalty for the murderers of policemen and prison guards than abolish it.
I also commend the 38 members of the government party who supported retention on second reading of the bill. I urge those 38 once again to give some thought to supporting this amendment. Even though it is not a good amendment, it is better than complete abolition. It reinstates the situation in which we are today, the five-year trial period. It will be up in December of 1977, at which time we can again make a decision when we have studied the results of the trial periods which existed from 1967 to 1972 and from 1972 to 1976.
Many members have said that this is a vote according to conscience and therefore it should be a free vote. As I said a minute ago, I admire the 38 members on the government side who voted against this bill on second reading. I think it was a free vote for them, but surely the cabinet's and the
Capital Punishment
parliamentary secretaries' votes do not suggest that they were allowed the same freedom given to the backbenchers in that party. Many members have quoted Burke in saying that they have the right to lead their constituents. In 1794 Burke, in a speech made in Bristol, England, said:
Your representative does not use his industry only but his judgment and he betrays instead of serving you if he sacrifices it to your opinion.
It has not generally been realized that Burke lost the election in 1794. I should like to point out that many hon. members may well lose the next election if they do not pay attention to the wishes of their constituents.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in the report stage debate on Bill C-84, not to reiterate what my colleagues and I have said with regard to the retention of capital punishment-I think we have stated our case very clearly-but rather as a matter of duty to plead with the government to heed the wishes of the majority of Canadians who have stated that they want the retention of capital punishment.
Can the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) tell this House why the bill must be debated now? Could it not have waited until after the Olympics? I feel the timing is insane. To debate the bill now does nothing but cast a shadow of apprehension over and doubt in the minds of those taking part in the Olympics as well as of those responsible for security at the games.
It appears that the government is strongly in favour of pampering criminals. Surely we must have our priorities confused. What are we doing to protect the citizens of Canada? Precious little, I would say, when we are making it harder for those responsible for maintaining law and order to carry out their duties. What we are doing is suggesting to Canadians that if the government does not invoke strong deterrents which will curb the ever increasing crime rate, the citizens of Canada will have to take the law into their own hands.
I have respect for all my colleagues on all sides of this House. However, I feel that the moral responsibility of hon. members is being overshadowed by their own personal feelings, which should not happen when in each constituency some 20,000 Canadians went to the polls to vote for the man or woman they felt would bring to parliament the opinions of the majority in their constituencies.
Some hon. members argue that this is a free vote which gives them the right to vote as they see fit regardless of the feelings of their constituents. What has happened? Has this session lasted too long? Are some hon. members that out of touch with reality?
July 8, 1976

To bring us back to reality I would like to read just one letter, out of hundreds I have received, from radio station CJOC in Lethbridge, dated June 28, as follows:
Dear Mr. Hurlburt:
This letter has to do with the capital punishment bill that went through second reading on Wednesday, June 23, 1976.
I decided that it was about time that the Government of Canada knew exactly what the people of Southern Alberta felt about the bill
On Wednesday, June 23 and Thursday, June 24 I opened the phone lines here at CJOC Radio to find out what the residents of Southern Alberta felt about capital punishment. The phone lines were opened between 1:30 and 5:30 p.m. both said days. The final vote read like this: FOR capital punishment-384 votes AGAINST capital punishment-18 votes
I also received some mail after the phone line vote was finished with. Enclosed are the letters I received.
I do hope that this will give you a little more backing in Ottawa knowing that 90% or more of Southern Alberta is right behind you as far as the capital punishment bill is concerned.
Adding the letter vote to the phone vote the final tally reads:
399 for capital punishment 18 against capital punishment
We here in Southern Alberta would appreciate it if you were to show this to either Mr. Trudeau himself, or someone that might care.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Regards,
Lethbridge Broadcasting Limited
I would also like to read a telegram from one of my constituents who happens to be an abolitionist, as follows:
Congratulations on your sturdy stand re law and order. Myself, an abolitionist of capital punishment by ideal, consider abolition presently the wrong measure, at the wrong time, in the wrong way, particularly remembering the coming Olympics. Good luck. G. R. C. Palmer, MD.
Dr. Palmer is from the city of Lethbridge.
For the life of me I cannot understand why the government thinks nothing of spending millions and millions of dollars on study group after study group-even study groups studying study groups-but when it comes to Bill C-84 it completely ignores the requests, wishes, and advice of our police forces across the entire country.
In conclusion, I think it behooves all of us to spend a few minutes reflecting on the wishes of our constituents.

Mr. Speaker, during the debate on Bill C-84, more precisely on May 11, I mentioned that I did not see any difference between the value of the life of a father or mother, a policeman or a prison guard or a defenceless citizen brutally attacked by bandits who are ever increasing in number. I might add that I have not changed my mind on this matter. However, I find that the motion under discussion is designed to give at least some protection needed by those who are responsible for the protection of society.
I know that policemen are better trained and prepared to defend themselves against bandits; on the other hand, they are much more exposed since their role is to try to arrest various types of criminals. And we notice from many examples that criminals are most of the time well armed and do not hesitate much before shooting down policemen on duty. The registration of their weapons is no problem at all for them. They have their own supply sources that are not subject to red tape which often lack flexibility. In view of the actual situation in general, we should at least give
Capital Punishment
law enforcement officers the assurance that the legislators realize the importance of their role and provide them with enough protection through legislation to cause those who are planning, often long in advance, some acts leading to crime, to think twice.
A release from the Public Service Alliance of Canada, dated June 24, 1976, said the following, and I think a few excerpts from that release would be in order. The executive secretary-treasurer referred to certain matters in the second paragraph of his letter, after making reference to the statement made on June 15, 1976, by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) in his speech in the House of Commons. I remember very well the recent reactions of some members opposite when the hon. member for Lot-biniere (Mr. Fortin) alluded to the speech of the Prime Minister. And yet, that is exactly what he did say. I have the text of his speech right in fromt of me. I am quoting:
I want to make it very clear that, if a majority of hon. members vote against abolition, some people are going to be hanged. Their death would be a direct consequence of the negative decision made by this House on this bill.
I now shall continue to quote from the letter of the executive secretary to the members of the House of Commons. It reads:
As for us, we appeal to your conscience and we take the opposite view of that expressed by Mr. Trudeau by saying that abolitionist would be responsible for all future murders of penitentiary employees and law enforcement officers, and we swear that each time one of these murders is committed, we shall impute them to all those who have supported the abolition of capital punishment.
Here are a few facts that you should consider in our opinon:
1-	The irresponsible attitude of penitentiary commissioners and directors before the pressure groups who visit the institutions;
2-	The lack of proper management by the authorities of most penal institutions in the country;
3-	The shocking convict classification system which endangers the life of penitentiary employees as well as the life of most convicts who only want to obey the rules they must follow during their prison term;
4-	The present lack of facilities to guarantee the protection and safety of the staff against habitual criminals who have nothing to lose because of the 25 years of imprisonment they would have to serve under Bill C-83.
For these reasons, the Hon. Warren Allmand, Solicitor General of Canada, who did not have the courage to reveal these facts to the members of the House of Commons, should, in all conscience, resign his ministerial responsibilities since he has lost the confidence of all penitentiary employees and all law enforcement officers in Canada.
We urge you, in your heart of hearts, to consider the safety of your family and that of penitentiary employees and law enforcement officers while reflecting on these words: "We want everyone to clearly understand that if most members of Parliament vote against the retention of the death penalty, people will be murdered. The death of these people would then be a direct result of the negative decision made by the House of Commons on this bill."
What our society needs is not an attitude of tolerance or permissiveness towards criminals but a return of everyone to spiritual and moral values. Let the murderes particularly return to them. Then, it will be easier to forego the death penalty. In the meantime, however, let there be no question of abolishing the right and the duty, through the civil and judicial authority, to take the lives of those who have too little respect for that of others.

We insist on the retention of capital punishment not in a spirit of revenge but of legal reparation for the greatest of crimes, and also to protect the lives of the people in the interest of the public and of order.
I already pointed out that the method of execution could be changed either for the gas chamber or any other method deemed appropriate. Considering the tremendous increase in the number of crimes of various types and the attitude of our leaders regarding the means available to reduce the number of crimes and allow a greater number of people to earn a decent living, a rather severe sentence must be maintained to give cause for reflection to those who, because of their behaviour, are likely to take the lives of others if they feel they stand in the way of their crimes.
It must be kept in mind that any individual who respects the life of his neighbour will never have to fear the death penalty if it is retained. In the part of the brief from the executive director of the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police dealing with the attitude expected from the Solicitor General, the following was mentioned, of which I would like to quote two paragraphs:
Such a philosophy is of deep concern to us, because even if the period proposed in Bill C-84 remains in effect, it involves a much greater threat and danger for our society, and more particularly the prison guards in our institutions.
In view of that attitude, we submit that the minimum sentence of 25 years, as proposed in Bill C-84, is a flagrant hoax since, to all intents and purposes, a convict will have the right to ask for a remission after his first 15 years in prison.
Recently, I read an article published in Quebec City's Le Soleil dated July 4, 1976. Take good note of the title:
U.S.A. Supreme Court Retains Capital Punishment
No fewer than 582 prisoners on death row, of whom 10 are women, from 30 different states, may be executed as a result of a long awaited decision of the Supreme Court.
By a majority of seven votes to two, the Supreme Court has rejected the request filed by the attorneys of six persons who were condemned to death after having been found guilty of murder in Florida, Louisiana, Texas, Georgia and North Carolina.
The attorneys did not deny the convicts' guilt, but they argued that the death penalty was a cruel and unusual punishment and therefore that it was unconstitutional. It was actually a test case for which the League for the Abolition of Capital Punishment tried to stir up public opinion.
Only Justices William Brennan and Thurgood Marshall were in disagreement with their seven other colleagues who rendered their decision after studying the files for three months. In their majority judgment, the justices considered that capital punishment was not unconstitutional.
I am surprised at the attitude of the Canadian abolitionists who usually keep abreast with the situation prevailing south of the border. They will probably answer that capital punishment has been abolished in several states. This parallel shows the necessity of retaining capital punishment considering that the majority of the Supreme Court judges after pondering over what has happened in the states where capital punishment has been abolished, are favourable to its retention in the states where it still exists.
From the strictly religious point of view, with respect to the concern of the accused for his fate in the hereafter, the murderer sentenced to death can always rely on the assistance of a religious adviser. If he wishes to, he can always beg for God's mercy and prepare himself to die. But his victims seldom have had such an opportunity. In concluding, let me quote from an article published in La Presse of
(Mr. Dionne (Kamouraska).]
June 2nd, 1976, and written by Mr. Arthur Piche; I may add that I agree with him.
Man has a right to life. Fine. But this is not equally true for the honest citizen and the murderer. To suggest the opposite would be denying a social and religious tradition which goes back to a thousand years and which has not yet been proved groundless or unfair even if abuses are unfortunately to be deplored. And when we say that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent against crime, we labour under a delusion.
Like anyone else, criminals fear death. It is evidenced by the fact that in order to protect themselves they carry arms and have often a whole stock of guns hidden somewhere.
And it has not been shown that a greater permissiveness and an absolute respect for the lives of murderers do help in curbing criminal activities. Indications would rather be to the contrary. We should therefore be wary of statistics purporting to show that the fear of death is not a deterrent, and that criminals do not value their own lives. If they do not why are we so concerned about saving them, once they are caught?
I also note that various press articles dealing with the subject illustrate on occasion what is going on. They should be food for thought to those who have the responsibility of deciding, because this is a very serious matter we are now discussing. I have here this other article that appeared in La Presse of April 17, 1975. It refers to the increasing rate of crime and the decreasing rate of case solving.
We would like some evidence that the government is making real efforts to try and reduce the crime rate in a way acceptable to the prople, to provide jobs and adequate salaries. But no, such evidence is lacking. In this country, we are living under a system that is totally upside-down. We are struggling between inflation and unemployment crises, without any solution whatsoever. It is that kind of situation that provides the ideal conditions under which discouraged people often feel compelled to do things that sometimes lead them to murder.
Clearly, in that kind of situation, over and above trying to improve the economic situation in Canada in general, and until there are more adequate ways of life, we must try and protect those who are paid to maintain law and order in Canada.

On May 22, 1973, I had to make a speech which, while not brief, was the most difficult I ever had to make. Certainly much preparation, thought and soul searching went into it. That speech dealt, as well, with
July 8, 1976

capital punishment. As you will recall, Your Honour, the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) had brought before the House a bill which would abolish capital punishment except in cases where a policeman or prison guard was the victim of murder. On that occasion I said the following:
For one thing, the minister-and I would predict, almost all of his cabinet colleagues-are abolitionists. Yet they present us with a bill that provides for the death penalty in the case of murder of a prison guard or law enforcement officer. If that alone is not questionable, surely the hypocrisy of this legislation is clear when the government presents us with a proposal it has no intention of carrying out. If a government is unable, or just plain unwilling to carry out legislation, it insults this House by presenting such legislation .. .
The present government would not enforce the penalty provided for in this legislation for the murder of a policeman or prison guard. To suggest it would do so is preposterous; to incorporate that suggestion into legislation is hypocritical.
I do not quote from my previous speech on this subject made when the Solicitor General brought forward the partial abolition bill because I want to claim credit as a prophet. It did not require powers of prophecy to see through the sham of the legislation he was presenting. I quoted my remarks to show that I understood the real designs of the Solicitor General and the government. Now, before the expiry of that experimental legislation which he claimed was so necessary and of paramount importance to the country, the Solicitor General says to us: "Let's wipe out the experiment. Let us forget what we promised with regard to another five-year period in which we would partially abolish capital punishment except in cases involving the murder of a policeman or prison guard. We are going to call the experiment off, abort the experiment in midstream, so to speak, and end capital punishment in this country." I say that the track record and attitude of the Solicitor General in matters concerning parliamentary democracy can only be viewed with deep regret.
It is interesting to note how government supporters proceeded when this bill was before the committee. When any ordinary piece of legislation is being considered, the members of this House, wishing to represent their constituents in the best way possible and not being experts in all fields, find it necessary to call witnesses to appear before a committee and to testify. Members hear what experts say about the application of this or that legislation. As I say, hon. members do not claim to be experts in highly controversial, difficult, and involved fields. We are a collection of commoners. Yet when this bill went to committee for study, the proposal of those opposing the bill to hear representatives of policemen and prison guards was turned down by the government majority on that committee.
